speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Ways and Means on the proposed resolution of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) respecting the taxation of excess profits; Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
Paragraph 2, let sub-paragraph, agreed to.
On paragraph 2, proviso "a":
Provided however-
(a) that the amount paid or payable by any person under the provisions of part one of the Special War Revenue Act, 1S15, shall be deducted from the amount which such person would otherwise be liable to pay, and the minister shall have power to determine any questions that may arise in consequence of any difference in the several periods for which the taxes under the said Act and those proposed herein are payable.

This is the enacting clause of the resolution, and it seems to be the proper clause upon which to hold any general discussion of the resolution. In' view of the fact that last night, before the committee rose, the minister, on being interrogated, intimated that he would consider any suggestions that might be made, I should like to point out the effect of the 'imposition of this tax upon every person connected with mining or kindred industries, where the enterprise involves the development of natural resources, and where the development cannot take place except by the employment of capital. The situation has been this.
During the past autumn, throughout Canada generally, there were a great many propositions promoted and on the verge of being capitalized through the assistance of foreign capital, and this legislation will seriously interfere with the consummation of any such capitalization. Indeed, the an-

no uncement which my hon. friend the minister made in his Budget speech about a month ago has had the effect of absolutely discouraging any attempt to promote industries of that kind. When a person with a proposition, no matter how good, goes abroad with the idea of obtaining the capital necessary for development, the possible investor inquires whether or not this is one of the companies which would be affected by the Budget of the Government. The person interested would be bound to tell the possible investor that it was one of those companies. It is well that persons should invest with the view of developing coal, silver, nickel, gold or other minerals. The person who invests in an enterprise of that kind, particularly at this stage of the world's history, does so with the hope of making some special profit. He takes bigger chances than are taken in the ordinary financial or industrial company. These deal with settled conditions. Business may vary or fluctuate; dividends may be small or great, but there is always a certain basis on which to proceed. It is the same with an industrial enterprise formed for the purpose of producing some special article used in the country. The production of the article is necessary to meet the needs of the people, and the person who invests in that industry knows that the question of receiving dividends depends upon his being able to produce the article as a saleable commodity, and that the price of the article will furnish him with a reasonable profit. But when a man goes into the mining industry, the conditions are entirely different. There may, or may not, be a large quantity of ore; all that has to be taken into consideration by the person who invests. To a very large degree the investment of capital in the mining industry is a gamble. If my hon. friend is going to throw into the melting pot these propositions, he will create a further menace which will intimate to the outside capitalist that the utmost he can get from his investment, after taking all chances, is 7 per cent, before the Government intervenes to take part of the profit. The minister will see that he is menacing the development of that industry everywhere. In addition to that, the party who is looking for capital [DOT] is not in a position to assure the possible investor that the Government may not, at a subsequent session, proceed to levy upon that class of industry to a greater degree. The minister may say, as he said last night, that this tax is going to last for only two vears. My hon. friend is not taking into
consideration, it seems to me, the very serious financial position which Canada is in as a whole when he invites us to believe that this or that or the other tax is going to stop at the end of two years. N The question of where taxation is going to end in this country, under our existing financial conditions, is a matter whch my hon. friend cannot determine, and he does well to put in a saving clause in regard to the future. The consequence is that the party looking for investment in a mining proposition cannot give any assurance that the tax will not be increased in the future, or that the percentage which is now taken is to be the limit.
For a moment, I might refer to that situation. It is all very well to be optimistic and to say that Canada will be in this or that position. There is no sign of the war ending. We do not know, even' in this House, all the commitments that we are making. We have not the information that we ought to have as to just how much this war is costing us to-day, or how much it has cost us since the last data was furnished to the House. Without that information we are in the dark. The extent of the. obligations which we may assume in the future is absolutely problematical and impossible to estimate. It seems to me that this House ought to have that information before taxation Bills and loan Bills are passed. I mention that incidentally to the point which I desire to make, that the party going to look for capital for a mining proposition cannot give assurances of any definite character that the percentage of profit, ito be taken from the man whose investment he desires, will be limited to that now proposed. That being so, the effect in regard to that particular industry is that it will be impossible for any one who has a mining proposition in this country to exploit it by obtaining the necessary capital for its development.
My hon. friend has gone so far as to put in an additional clause in the Bill which means that in determining the amount to be paid by a mining proposition the extent of the exhaustion of the ore in the ground will be taken into consideration. That is only so far so good. It minimizes the situation, but to a very infinitesimal degree. Mining is a natural industry in this country, quite as much so as agriculture. We all hope and believe that, particularly in the far northern country, there is an illimitable store of minerals, the development of which will mean a tremendous expenditure for

supplies and the increased prosperity of the country at large. This industry stands apart, as I have said, from the ordinary industrial and financial industries. It requires spec-ial consideration. I submit that the minister's proposal menaces the future of this industry, and that the slight amendment which he has made in no wise does away with the possibility of injury.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am really obliged to my hon. friend from Pictou for bringing up this matter for discussion. I need not say that I appreciate the benefit of his views upon any subject that may be under debate in this House. He has put forward his representations very temperately, and I propose to answer them as fully and frankly as I may be able. I think that my hon. friend and those connected with the mining industry, or I should rather say some of them, are unduly apprehensive as to the effect of this measure upon their industry. The Government is fully aware of the extreme importance of that industry in the national economy of Canad.a. It is one of the great natural industries, as my hon. friend has observed, and, certainly, the Government would be the last to take any step unless indispensably necessary in the national interest which might have the effect of in any way injuring the mining industry, or retarding the flow of capital into this country. I think I shall be able to, show before I take my seat that there is no ground for apprehension on the part of the mining community. This tax is, as I stated last night, for a limited period. My hon. friend questions whether I was justified in making that statement. I certainly was justified in making that statement, because it represents the intentions of the Government.
If you need money, what are you going to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am coming to that. My hon. friend says that the war may he prolonged for two or three years. For myself, I can scarcely see how that is possible. But it may be possible. But should the war be prolonged for the next two or three years, and the financial responsibility of the Government correspondingly increased, it would then, undoubtedly, be necessary to take such measures as might be expedient in the public interest to meet the situation which we should then-be confronted with. That statement is in no way inconsistent with that which I made last evening, namely, that this particular 
measure is for a period only. The principle of the resolutions, it would appear to me, indicates that. The principle of the-resolutions is in effect that those individuals, firms and companies, which since the outbreak of the war have been able to maintain a rate of profit beyond what we have fixed upon as a fair and normal prewar standard, shall contribute a fraction of that excess for the purposes of the war. It is a fact with regard to many businesses in Canada that the largest profits resulting from the war, either directly or indirectly, have been made, during the 18 months since the outbreak of the war, by reason of the increase in the price of commodities, due to the demand which arose by reason of the outbreak of hostilities, and in supplying of munitions and other requirements in connection with the war itself. I do not mean to say that if the war goes on there will be a less demand for commodities and munitions, but I do not think that, as the country becomes better organized to meet the new conditions, the prices which obr tained during the past 18 months will obtain in the future. Therefore, it would seem to me that I am perfectly justified in stating, as I do, on behalf of the-Government, that this is a temporary tax. In- making that statement, I largely meet the argument of my hon, friend that capital might be discouraged from embarking upon Canadian enterprise. It is hardly conceivable that an enterprise could be-established within the next few months, and before the termination of this legislation, earn such large net profits that the moderate tax which we are taking from them would be -a serious matter to the individual, firm, or company in question. Therefore, I do not believe, for myself, that when it is realized, as I believe it is now realized, that thi-s is a temporary measure, the effect which my hon. friend anticipates will be produced, or will continue, if such an effect has already been produced.
My hon. friend has, I think, made a statement which, if made by a responsible minister of the Government, would do more to retard the flow of capital through this country than this Budget. But as he is not .speaking on the authority of the Government, it will not have that effect. My hon. friend has clearly indicated the view that the war will probably be prolonged for a considerable period. As to that, I do not know that the information of any one is better than that of another. Itiis not for us to guess or speculate as to the-

length of the war. I never believed that the war would be a short war, but, on the other hand, I do not believe that it can be unduly prolonged. It would seem to me that if the war should continue for a period of, let us say two or three years more, civilization would almost be destroyed, and the economic resources of the world would almost disappear. I believe that long before any such date, as my hon.' friend has in his mind, the forces at work, making for the conclusion of this war, will be such that it will be concluded, and concluded on the terms we are contending for; because although the German nation has apparently been winning victories on land, it has Teally been losing the war. This war will be determined in the last analysis by superiority in resources, in men, in munitions, and in money.

The Minister of
Labour does not think we are going to win?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think he
does; I know he does. I happen to know that the Minister of Labour is certain we will win. The Government is certain we are going to win; not only that, but we are going to leave no stone unturned to make certain that we shall win. That, among other reasons is my motive in bringing down this budget. I want those who can afford to pay, to pay. There is no one who will be taxed that cannot afford to pay, and I know of no one who is not willing to pay. Iii fact, I know the people are anxious to pay the tax [DOT]imposed by this budget.
This measure, therefore, being a temporary measure, it is not conceivable to me, when it is understood, that it will have any effect in retarding the flow of capital towards this country. Let us assume for a moment, however, that it would; let us assume that my hon. friend is right, and that it would have some effect in retarding the flow of capital to this country. I ask this House, would that be a good reason for a Government refraining from faking any taxation action that it might deem indispensible towards the winning of this war. Suppose that at the time of the war between the North and the South, when the United States was torn in twain, it had /been suggested for a moment that the proposals of the Secretary of the Treasury designed, and necessary, for the prosecution of the war by the North,, would have the effect of retarding the flow of
capital into the, United States; would such a suggestion have been listened to seriously? In Canada tb-day, does anyone consider seriously whether general business is going to be impaired or not? General business is of extreme importance. I yield to no man in my desire that the Government should carry on this war with a minimum of inconvenience to the business of the community. I desire that the war should be carried on, in so far as we can carry it on, with our full power, in such a way as to interfere in the least possible degree with the business activities of this country. I desire that on the grounds of business itself, but I desire it more strongly on the ground that, the more we can promote business, the greater the industrial and commercial activities of the country, the better will we 'be able to sustain the economic burden of the war. Therefore, in answer to my hon. friend I may say that while I do not believe that the effect of this legislation will be to retard the flow of capital to this country, I am bound to say that the first duty of this country is the conduct of the war, and that business considerations, while of great importance, are really secondary; and I believe the public in this country take that view. I believe that the public takes that view.
What is the object of this taxation? I have been talking, members of both sides of the House have been talkifig, and with the greatest sincerity, of the seriousness of this war, and there is no divided opinion as to the reality of the menace to the Empire and to Canada. We all have supreme confidence that the issue will be decided in our favour, but we have been alive to the peril, and, so far as I have been able to observe, hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, hold the view that we must put forth the utmost efforts in order to bring about the results which we believe will be brought about, namely, ultimate and conclusive victory. We have been talking about liberty, civilization, and religion being in the crucible, and about the safety of Canada and the integrity of the Empire being menaced by this German peril. We believe that. We are so remote, fortunately in one sense, unfortunately in another, from the scene of the conflict that it is not possible for us, with all the imagination we possess, to visualise what is going on in Europe. You would, not hear any
What company was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will give my
hon. friend the names privately. These gentlemen would not like to have their names mentioned in the House. My hon. friend is apprehensive about the mining industry. I think he has totally miscalculated the effect of the Bill upon that industry. The principle of the taxation is this: If net profits have been made, in the case of companies, including mining companies, in excess of 7 per cent, we take one-quarter of the excess and one-quarter only. Does my hon. friend know that, excluding nickel companies, only twenty-four mining companies in the whole Dominion paid dividends last year? My authority is the Canadian Mining Journal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are not very prosperous, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The extraordinary thing is that some were exceedingly prosperous.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Only the
twenty-four are prosperous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Others are engaged in the business, but they are not affected by this tax, and many of these are not affected by the tax. The point I am making is that the mining industry has nothing seriouls to apprehend from this tax. We are fighting for this country, we are fighting for every business in it, including mining. On what principle can I, or can the Government, leave out mining industries from the operation of this tax? On what principle can I tax a manufacturing company, a transportation Company, a trading company and pass by the Hollinger mines worth $10,000,000, or $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 and earning up to $2,000,000 net profits? On what principle can I pass by the Nipissing mine earning $1,200,000 a year and worth brobably $5,000,000. How can I pass by copper companies in view of the fact that copper has doubled in price since the outbreak of the war? On what principle can I pass by the nickel companies -which are making enormous sums out of the natural resources of the country? I appreciate to the full what the mining industry at Cobalt and Porcu-

pine means to the province of Ontario and I appreciate the importance of the mining industry to British Colnm'bia, but the point I make is that the mining industry is not going to, be injured materially by this legislation and I shall show my hon. friend from Pictou that he has misjudged the effect of the legislation upon these mining companies.
I do not believe there is a country in the world in which lefes revenue is derived from mining than Canada. Take the highly mineralized area in Northern Ontario, Cobalt and Porcupine and other mineralized areas; I was surprised to-find the other day that the entire amount of revenue derived by the province of Ontario from its mineral areas was about $300,000. It cannot be sqid that in so far as Canada is concerned there is anything in the situation that would retard the flow of capital towards this country for the purpose of embarking in the mining industry. The Minister of Mines of British Columbia was here the other day and I inquired of him how much revenue they derived from the mines of British Columbia. He informed me that they got $150,000. I do not know of any country in the world in which such small amounts are taken from the mining industry by way of royalty 'and taxation as in Canada. I do not believe that the imposition of this moderate tax is going to have the effect, amongst a community as intelligent as the mining community of causing them to slacken their efforts in the development of that great natural resource. We go to the legislation of the United States; the United States is a great mineral country and yet there has been an income tax imposed not only upon the subsidiary mining companies but upon the holding companies. The maximum allowance made by the United States'for exhaustion of capital is only five per cent. I think that is too small, and I shall deal with that phase a little later on. Take the nickel companies of Canada. The International Nickel Company, which has its refining plant in the United States and operates, I believe, through a subsidiary company at Sudbury, had earnings of nearly $10,000,000 for the nine months ended December 31, 1915. Now I do not believe that public opinion would sustain the Government in taxing all other industries in Canada and passing by these mining companies.
Was it the International Nickel Company or the Canada Copper Company that earned the $10,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The International Nickel Company. I mentioned the subsidiary company at Sudbury, which is called,
I believe, the Canada Copper Company. I give that as an illustration of the large earnings of these mining companies, and I am going to show later tnat the amount we shall take from these mining companies is so small that it will have no appreciable effect on the mining industry at all. Only comparatively few mining companies in Canada are subject to the tax, and they will contribute very much less than my hon. friend has in view. The mining companies desire to contribute. Some of them would rather that the tax was on a basis so that they would not have to contribute so much; that is no doubt very natural. I hear there are also -a few, but very few, who would rather not pay anything at all. But we should not be justified in acceding to their request and exempting them from the operation of this tax, provided of course that they made large profits. I can say this: that those in the mining industry who do not desire to pay are decidedly in the minority; the great majority do want to pay; they recognize it as just that they should pay, and among these I am happy to say are the Americans.
Let us for a moment consider the principle of the application of this measure to the mining industry. I admit that it is [DOT]more difficult to apply a measure of this kind to mining companies than tb manufacturing, industrial or commercial business. The reason is that mining, as my hon. friend from Pictou has pointed out, is a calling in which there are many disappointments, and in which abnormal profits must be looked for. I think that is generally admitted. A man who might be quite content with seven per cent in a manufacturing business would not invest in a mining company upon the basis of a seven per cent return on his investment. It must be borne in mind that a man who speaks of getting say twenty per cent in a mining company, especially a company that is operating metalliferous mines, knows that in that twenty per cent there is a large return of his capital each year. That is among the reasons why, in mining, a larger return is required than in the case of an ordinary commercial or indus-

trial enterprise. The same remark would apply to other businesses-I do not say that twenty per cent would apply-in which the capital invested is depleted from year to year. The resolution I have brought down relates net profits to capital. I would call the attention of my hon. friend from Pictou to the fact that in the resolution originally brought down we used the term " net profits." I may say that mining had not escaped our attention, and for this reason, among others: We had examined carefully the American income tax legislation-, in which provision is made for an allowance for exhaustion or depletion oi capital not to exceed five per cent of the gross output in any one year. It did not appear to us that we should place a limit of that kind upon the amount that we should allow for exhaustion of capital. There are. some mines whose average life is eight or ten years. I am speaking of metalliferous mines. Then other -mines, such as coal mines, last for generations, and the same considerations,except in a general way, do not apply; that is to say, the percentage of exhaustion in a coal mine in a particular year is not so great as the amount of exhaustion in connection with metalliferous mines such as gold, silver and copper mines. We therefore deemed it improper to place any limit on the percentage which we should allow for exhaustion of the capital of a mine. In the administration of this Act it may be necessary for us in some cases to say we shall allow ten, twelve or thirteen per cent; and in other cases five, or two per cent. It all depends upon the character of the mine with which we are dealing. The hon. member for Pictou will, I am sure, concede that if we tax what are known as profits and distributed to shareholders, say under the mining laws of the province of Ontario, but which are really not net profits, and deduct from those profits a proper amount, as we should be entitled to do under the provisions of this Act, for depreciation of plant and machinery, and for exhaustion, in the case of some mines, to the extent of ten, twelve or more per cent of the value of the mine, they take on a very different complexion from what are ordinarily understood as profits in the payment of dividends to shareholders in mining companies. The result of dealing with the profits of mining companies in that way- and it is a proper way to deal with them- will be to make the net profits appear to he much smaller than the apparent profits which are published from time to time. So much for that phase. I have not considered [Sir Thomas White !
it necessary to place any limit in the Act, because I think in its administration the judgment of the officials should be left unfettered, although, of course, they will have to act on some principle which will be fair to all. I do not, however, consider it necessary to fix in the Bill a limit of percentage to be allowed for the exhaustion of mines. I have dealt with the matter of net profits, and it does seem to me that in dealing with them in that way we are placing the mining industry on a parity with all other industries.
Now we come to another question, which I am sure my hon. friend from Pictou has given attention to: the question of capital, of reserve, rest and accumulated profits. My hon. friend will observe, by an amendment I shall make to the resolution, that "may" will become "shall."
In all companies?'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had great difficulty, I confess, in reaching a conclusion upon that point. I derived substantial advantage in reaching my conclusion from the discussion in this House. I have no small vanities which would make me disclaim the advantages received from a discussion in a House such as this. A minister brings down a comprehensive measure of taxation. He knows that it is more or less rough-hewn, and that he will obtain much more information after he brings it down than -he had when it was-drafted.. As long as the principle of a Bill is correct, inequalities can be corrected in this House, and a minister must be prepared to act in ithe light of information that he may receive from hon. members. I would call the attention of my hon. friend from Pictou to the fact that, in estimating capital we shall -have regard, not only to capital stock, but to rest, reserve, and accumulated profits. These will all be embraced under capital.
My hon. friend from Pictou is a lawyer, and I desire to make this statement to him. If we had proceeded absolutely logically we should have said: We will take the value of all the assets, real and personal, movable and immovable, of every company, firm and individual in Canad,a, and subtract the liabilities from the assets and the difference will be t-he capital. I need not, however, tell the House that that would be a Herculean task for the officials charged with the administration of this measure. In -the case of most companies the capital, reserve, and accumulated profits are accurately stated, in their reports, and one

would feel perfectly safe in taking their statement where the capital stock has been paid in full: capital, so much; reserve and accumulated profits, so much, representing premium on the price of stock sold to shareholders, or profits which have been taken into reserve, or contingent fund, or allowed to jemain in profit and loss account. So in the case of an ordinary company for the sake of taxation, you have your capital, your reserve or rest account, and your accumulated, profits, substantially representing the capital of the. company invested in that business.
The gross capital?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the net.
What about the liabilities?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I am right. I am speaking of capital, reserve and accumulated profits only; I am not speaking of the total assets. I say that that substantially represents the capital of that company. Just as an individual has invested in a business $100,000 which would represent the value of its assets less its liabilities, so, in determining what the capital of a company logically is, you would say: What is the - value of its assets and what are its liabilities? You would then deduct the liabilities from the assets and in that way get the capital. If the business of a company has been conducted properly, if the stock has been all paid in cash, you will find that that will correspond with capital stock, rest, reserve and accumulated profits.
Mining companies present difficulties in ascertaining the capital invested in them, because there is no necessary connection between the nominal capital of a mining company and its real capital, which is the value of its mines. Therefore, you will find, these anomalies. You will 4 p.m. find a company incorporated some years ago, say, with a capital of $250,000 or $500,000, and you will find that the property to-day may be worth $5,000,000; that a holding company has probably been created, holding the stock in the original company, now the subsidiary company of the holding company, and that the dividends are being paid, say, at the rate of 15 or 20 per cent upon a capital of $5,000,000. Now, this taxation will apply, of course, to the underlying company; but it will be necessary, in order to be perfectly fair to the mining industry, that in considering what its capital is, under the provisions of this Bill, you have regard to the amount of its fully paid up capital and to the values of its reserves, rest and accumulated property, the three together, as I have stated, representing substantially the value of the mine. In my opinion, that is absolutely fair and just, and it is the principle that would be applied to financial institutions, private individuals and firms in business. The first question is:	What is the
true amount of your capital? The second is: What is the true amount of your net profits ? Now, relate your net profits to the true amount of your capital and you will easily be able to make the calculations called for in this measure. Therefore, I think, in view of the statement I have made, that the apprehensions of those engaged in the mining industry that this tax is going to be oppressive, will be allayed, if not entirely removed, because, on the one hand, the so-called profits are cut down to a net basis, and on the other hand, the capital, reserve and accumulated profits are deemed to be the value of the property, less the liabilities, of course, that is, the true capital invested in the enterprise.
I do not, at the moment, desire to say anything further than this, that, if these resolutions and the Bill which I shall introduce later should meet, as I believe they will, with the approval of this House, it will be our object to administer this legislation, while strictly, in accordance with the legislation, with good judgment and with scrupulous fairness to all parties concerned. The administration will be under the Department of Finance, the tradition of which I believe has been good, and I certainly desire to pass it on unimpaired. It has been suggested here that political con siderations might enter into the adminis tration of this measure. I do not believe that that view is shared in by a majority of the members of this House, nor that it is shared in by hon. gentlemen opposite. We are bringing in an exceptional measure under exceptional conditions, and the House realizes the fact that this is a Bill that under normal conditions would not be brought down. I am sure hon. members will have confidence that this measure will be administered fairly and justly to all parties concerned, and most certainly without regard to political considerations in order that the end may be accomplished that we have in view in introducing this measure, namely, that we may raise a substantial amount of revenue to cover our expenditures in connection with the war.

Perhaps I have spoken longer than a minister should in committee; but the hon. member for Pictou, I know, is sincerely interested in this matter; he has a wide interest in mines; he is sympathetic to the mining industry; he is well informed; he has put forward his views; he has raised questions; he has made representations, and I have thought that his desire was that I should deal with this matter, so that those engaged in the mining industry may be reassured as to certain matters about which they have been in doubt, namely as to what net profits mean and as to what capital means in connection with their industry.
There is another thing. My hon. friend has touched upon the question of the certainty of a tax. It is a good principle in taxation that those who are liable to pay a tax should be able, within reasonable bounds, to ascertain what the tax will mean, because in many cases, they make their future arrangements accordingly. Now, this Bill should be through this House in the course of the next couple of weeks-at least I am hoping it will-and once it becomes law, there will be no difficulty whatever, because the legislation will begin to operate at once, if any mining company is [DOT] desirous of ascertaining what its taxation will be, in making their return and having the officials of the department check it over and make an assessment upon it. I think we should be able to begin making our assessment in May. Returns will he called for in May or June, or, if any are unduly apprehensive about the amount they will have to pay, they can easily ascertain substantially what it will amount to.
Again I thank my hon. friend from Pictou for giving me an opportunity to make this statement.

If I criticise some of the points in this Bill, I want it distinctly understood that I am not in any way opposing the taxation of corporations. I do not believe that any hon. member on this side objects to the taxation of corporations, but we criticise the inequality of the taxation. Under this Bill, one man is taxed, while two or three others who should be equally liable are not reached at all. Suppose a man hae $100,000 invested in a mercanatile business, he is taxed; but his next door neighbour has $500,000 invested in some other way, and no attempt is made to take a dollar from him. If a man has his money invested in bonds, securities, or real estate, from which he derives a big 
income, the Minister of Finance does not make the slightest attempt to get at him. And that is the reason vdiy this Bill, in my judgment, when it comes to be understood, will not be popular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
understands, of course, that this tax
*
applies only to companies making over seven per cent profit; it is a tax, not upon capital, but upon profits beyond a certain amount. I explained that last night.
I understand that perfectly. But what I object to is that -the man who has millions invested, -and is making more than seven per cent on his investment-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do they make that?

If he is not making more than seven per cent, he is making far more in amount than the man with $250,000 in a commercial business that may be making over seven per cent; yet he is not called upon to pay a single dollar. I was not here last night, but I understand -that the objection offered by the Minister of Finance to an income tax was the difficulty of collecting it, and the fact that many would escape. To my mind, it would not be a bit more difficult to collect an income tax than it will be to collect the. tax imposed under this Bill. This will be an expensive matter, and you will only get at a certain small proportion of the community, whereas, if the tax were evenly distributed over the wealth of the country, and every man who -has wealth, who 'has an income, were called upon to pay, the tax would not fall so heavily upon our industries.
The Minister of Finajice has just spoken about the capitalization of mines. I am not sure that I clearly understood what he said. Suppose that a mining company, organized a few years ago, has a paid-up capital of $250,000. They bought a property for $100,000 and spent $150,000 in plant and in carrying on the business. Between tnat time and the time when this tax comes into effect they make a fine discovery of ore, so that the mine, instead of being worth $100,000,'is worth $1,000,000. In that case, is that $1,000,000 capital, or is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Assuming that $1,000,000 is a proper valuation in the opinion of experts, then I should say the true position of that company would be this:

Its capital is $250,000, and its reserve, rest, and accumulated profits make up the balance. Its capital, for the purposes of this Act, would be $1,000,000.

That is what I was not clear about. Now, the Minister of Finance discussed the nickel companies, and spoke of the readiness of the American owners of mines to pay their share of these taxes. Will he. say that the International Nickel Company will pay taxes under this legislation? For my part, I do not see how it is possible for the minister to tax that company. He may tax their subsidiary company, the Canada Copper Company. The minister has just stated that these companies are making vast sums of money, the price of copper having doubled. But the minister will find himself practically up against a stone wall in the case of the Canada Copper Company, for that is a subsidiary company. It d,oes not sell 'ore, nor does it sell the finished nickel. It roasts and smelts the ore at Copper Cliff, near Sudbury, and turns out a matte which is shipped to the International Nickel Company. It does not make the slightest difference to the Canada Copper Company what it charges for the matte. Our nickel goes into the United States and is refined in New Jersey, and the company is making millions. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) said the other night that it was making $5,000,000, but the Minister of Finance said that a subsidiary company was making $10,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the main company.	'
Then that makes it very clear. The Minister of Finance says they make $10,000,000, and the Solicitor General the other day said they made $5,000,000.
That was last year.
They were talking within a week of each other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I read from the Canadian Mining Journal:
The International Nickel Company, in the three months ended December 31, 1913, earned some $3,423,246 ; and in the nine months ended December 31, 1915, earned $9,741,828.
-We have not the figures for last year.

I would recommend my hon. friend to give that information to his colleague, the Solicitor General, who, in order to turn an argument, stated that their profits were $5,000,000. But the point
I want to make is that my hon. friend is not able to tax the International Nickel Company; he cannot possibly tax them. While' our own people have to pay the tax, these gentlemen, living across the line, who take our ore over there, refine it over there, 1 keep 2,000 men at work all the year round, and have all their big-salaried men in the state of New Jersey, cannot be taxed one dollar under this legislation. My * hon. friend will not make any attempt to tax them, simply because he cannot do it under this legislation. Then there is their . subsidiary company, the Canada Copper Company. Copper has gone up, as my hon. friend has stated, to double the price it was a short time ago. Nickel has gone up, in spite of all the Solicitor General has said, to practically double the price it was two years ago. Allied nations in Europe are offering almost fifty cents a pound for nickel, and are willing to make long contracts for it. The price of nickel is practically double what it was before the war. You cannot get at the profits of the Canada Copper Company to tax them to any extent, simply because they are only a subsidiary company, and it does not make any difference to the shareholders whether they sell their matte for five cents a pound or for fifteen cents a pound-the profits are made on the American end.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not at all agree with my hon. friend's conclusion.
I think the Bill has a provision that will meet the case in point.

I hope that is the case. If we can tax the International Nickel Company, I shall be very much pleased, because if there is any one institution in this country that ought to pay a tax of this kind, it is that particular company, who take our ore out of Canada to the United States, refine it there, sell it to our opponents-not directly, but indirectly-scatter it all over the world, and make huge profits. If my hon. friend can so word his Bill as to tax a company' organized in the United States, operating in the United States, whose dividends are distributed in the United States, I shall be most delighted to hear it. But it seems to me he wall have quite a contract on his hands to collect the tax from the gentlemen who are now so anxious to say that they want to pay a share of it. I venture to say a good many of them are saying that with the knowledge that they cannot be taxed. At all

events, if they can be taxed it will be a very good thing.
My hon. friend states that this is a war tax. I hope that it is a war tax, and that every dollar of it that will be collected will go to the war funds. But we have to take that statement with a little grain of salt; because my hon. friend last year told us that the direct taxes he then imposed were war taxes. My hon. friend said that the extr-a cent imposed on letters and post cards was for war purposes, and that every time a man, woman, or child in Canada bought 10 cents worth of stamps during the past year the additional revenue went to the war fund. But what was the result? From what I have heard in the House during this session, the Post Office Department stole it all from the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.
They did not turn it over to the Government; they kept it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They did not.
Will my hon. friend say that the Government got, for war purposes, all the extra revenue from the sale of those stamps?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The entire revenue of the Post Office Department, like that of all other departments of the Dominion, finds its way into consolidated revenue fund; and every dollar of taxation that was collected last year, either by indirect or by direct taxation, was us'ed for the purposes of the war, as well as a very large additional sum.

That is no information. I am quite certain that large sums other than those collected as revenue were used for the war. But the extra expenses of the Post Office Department have more than eaten up the extra revenue from the sale of postage stamps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Supposing that the extra postal taxation had not been imposed, would the additional expenditure of the Post Office Department not have had to be paid out of consolidated revenue fund?

Well, yes. If that had been the case, the deficit would have been double what it is; that is the only difference. The deficit in the Post Office Department, I understand, will be something like $3,000,000 this year. If my hon. friend had not passed this measure last year, exacting an extra 50 per cent postage, the deficit in the Post Office Department would have been about $6,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would it not have had to be paid out of consolidated revenue fund? Of course, it would.

If it had not been fpi
the extra revenue from the sale of postage stamps, my hon. friend the Postmaster General would not have been so extravagant. There was absolutely no necessity of'expending all the money that was expended. While on that subject, I want to say that if this Government would use the slightest economy, if they would economise in any degree at all, one-half the revenue which my hon. friend proposes to raise at the present time would not be necessary at all.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend from
Halton laughs, but why should it be necessary this year to spend 50 per cent more in running the country than was expended 4 or 5 years ago? Why should it be necessary? We were not at war at that time, we had a buoyant revenue, and there might have been some excuse for large expenditures; but to-day, when we have the greatest war of history on our hands, when we are called upon to provide tens of millions of dollars every [DOT] year for interest, and when the ordinary revenue has fallen very materially owing to the influence of the war, the Minister of Finance claps on full sail and goes ahead; he does not try to economise in the slightest degree, judging by the amounts he is asking for at this present session. What is wanted is not so much this tax Bill as some little economy on the part of the Government; if they would economize to any reasonable degree at all, it would not be necessary to have all this direct taxation. If we have got to have more revenue, I quite agree that it is best to raise it by direct taxation. I woulld like to see my hon. friend take some steps to make that taxation apply fairly equally. I do not suppose that it can be applied with absolute equality, but it should apply fairly equally to thoee who have money and are able to pay. It is very extraordinary that the Government should adopt a system of this kind when, in this very city of Ottawa, there are over a dozen millionaires, several of them multimillionaires, walking around with revenues of upwards of $100,000 per annum. Yet my hon. friend does not make the slightest effort to take a single dollar from one of them. It is the struggling man in business who is being taxed, and the .wealthy

concerns, in a general way, are going to escape. That is how it will work out to a very large extent. While I quite agree with the taxation of corporations, I would have liked to have seen some system of equality by which all would be taxed somewhat alike.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion, the Budget is a very fair one. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) in his usual-shall I .say-reckless fashion-
Say what you wish.
Then I shall say reckless fashion-
Free speech.

-attempts to show this House that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in bringing down this Budget is not taxing the moneyed man. In my opinion this Budget covers very largely the class that we want to get after, the class that is able to pay. As to the individual and the question of an income tax, the reason is apparent why this Government has not undertaken to impose taxation along that line. I am not going to take up the time of the committee this afternoon at any length; hut I simply wish to say that when the Budget was first brought down I was of the opinion that the taxation wa3 going to bear very heavily upon the mining industry. Knowing that capital is easily frightened, and especially such capital as seeks investment in the mining industry, I was much alarmed at the thought that it was possible and probable that this Budget as applied to mining companies would have the effect of keeping capital out of our country.	The difficulty of mining is
not so much to get capital for the mine of known value; it is to get capital for the prospect, for the undeveloped mine, because once you have a mine developed- there is nothing in the way of getting ample capital to operate it, because you can always show -rile profits that can be made. I interviewed my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and discussed the question with him, and he agreed with me that the mining industry was entitled to greater consideration than was an ordinary commercial company. The ordinary commercial company, if it is well managed, is in a better position after it has been operated for a number of years to make money than when it first started in, because it has established a reputation and is in a
position to do business appertaining to its particular line much better than when it commenced. The mining company, on the other hand, is producing something from the ground, and every ton of ore that is produced and marketed is just so much depreciation of its capital. The life of metalliferous mines is anywhere from 5 to 25 years; in some districts the life of a mine is much longer than it js in others owing to the geological formation which results in the ore bodies extending to a greater depth. The Minister of Finance has provided for that, and his proposition, as outlined this afternoon to me, is an eminently fair one. I have no hesitation in saying that I believe it will be acceptable to the mining interests of the province from which I come and the mining interests of Canada generally. There has been a great deal of misunderstanding as to just how this tax is going to be applied in connection -with mining companies, but from the explanation we have had this afternoon I think that that misunderstanding will be removed. I am further of the opinion that there is no mining company, in the province of British Columbia at least, that would seek to evade taxation for war purposes entirely. I believe they are all quite ready and willing to pay their fair share of the tax. They are just as confident of a satisfactory conclusion to this war as we are and just as ready to pay their proportion of the cost.
While on this subject, might I digress to say that the war has been very beneficial to the mining industry of Canada? I am not speaking now so much of the additional price obtained for the product, but of the fact that it has made the people of Canada and Great Britain, as well as this Government, see the necessity that exists for the reduction and refining of ores within our own community. The Government have arranged for the reduction and refining of zinc. An arangement is being made, I believe, for the refining of copper, and I am going to express the hope that the Government will never rest until they see that every pound of gold, silver, lead, zinc, copper and nickel produced in the Dominion is also refined within our own country and sold as finished products.

As my hon. friend
comes from British Columbia, could he tell me whether or not we have any actual refining of copper and lead here, or if we produce any of these minerals in a mercantile condition for sale?

I cannot speak for the
Bast, but we have in the West, and have had for some time, a plant that reduces and refines lead and all the silver, copper and gold that may be contained within the lead product. We have in operation in British Columbia the electrolytic process for the reduction of zinc. It is producing electrolytic zinc, which is a very pure form of zinc and does not contain over .two-tenths of one per cent of impurities. That plant is in operation to-day and is being extended. It is at present producing 25 tons per day, but they propose to extend it to treat all the zinc ores that they can possibly handle. There is no copper being refined as such within Canada as far as I know. We do not go any further than bringing the copper into matte, or blistering it. I believe arrangements are now being made, and that a plant has been erected to refine in Canada as much copper as the home market will absorb, and I am in hopes that the Government will not rest until all metals produced in Canada are refined in this country.
Would my hon. friend give us the capacity of the copper refining plant which is now nearing completion?

I think that we produce in Canada to-day something like 60,000,000 pounds of copper. The manager of the works in question told me that their plant would provide for the normal consumption of Canada, which would be nine or ten million pounds a year. I do not think I can add anything further, except to repeat that I am sure the mining industry of British Columbia will be satisfied with this taxation after the explanation given by the minister this afternoon.

I am very glad that my kon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Green) has corroborated a statement which I made early in the discussion to-day, as to the danger that might arise from imposing a tax upon the mining industry. While the minister's explanation, that the value of the metal in the ground, is to be considered as a portion of the capital upon which earnings have to be made before the tax is imposed, may relieve in some measure the fears of those who are interested in operating mines, yet it does not remove the fears that exist in the minds of those who may be approached for capital for the purpose of developing a mine whose real value has not been ascertained. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance states that this

is a temporary measure only, and not a final solution of the question. He may say that in the Bill he does not propose to make t'he tax applicable for a. longer period than two years; but when 1 suggested that the obligations imposed as a result of this war might not be concluded at the end of two years, my hon. friend proceeded to indulge in a lot of sidewind talk about the war, which was wholly irrelevant. I made no prediction as to how long this war was going to last. I could not predict that any more than my hon. friend could. It is not the exact date upon which this war will finish that will decide how long this country is to be taxed, but these two things will determine it; first, the extravagance of my hon. friend, and, secondly, the obligations imposed by the war. My hon. friend's extravagance is still going on this year. He said last night that the only way we could get money was by saving. I would point out that the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain has set an example by giving up his motor car and walking from Westminster to Downing street every morning. My hon. friend's idea of economy is to include in the Estimates $28,000,000 which he says he will not expend unless a supervening necessity-which might be a political question-arises.	Whether we should all be
in a sound financial position at the end of two years depends in the first place, upon whether the minister practices the economy he preaches; and, secondly, upon the amount of money we spend upon the waT. Although we have been sitting for two [DOT] months the Minister of Finance has not yet given to the House the total cost of the war to date, nor how much it is costing us each day. We agreed to my hon. friend taking power yesterday to borrow $75,000,000, and we have before us now proposals which are intended to raise a very large sum of money. And I say that before my hon. friend should ask this House and investors to believe that this taxation is to be purely temporary, he should give us a statement of how much we have paid on account of the war, and, secondly, he should set us an example in economy.
My hon. friend told us that nobody in England had raised any question in regard to the proposals made in the British House for carrying on the war. I venture to say that if my hon. friend will read the English Hansard he will find that the question how the money should be Taised there is a

matter of free discussion. My hon. friend must not think, simply and solely because he and his colleagues happen to be in power while the war is on, that everything the Government proposes must be ratified, and that free people in this House are guilty of lese majeste if we venture to criticise the Government's proposals, and suggest better methods of meeting our obligations. That attitude is entirely erroneous.
The Minister of Finance says, in an apologetic way, that this taxation is purely temporary, and that for the purpose of raising a certain amount of money this year he is putting a tax on industry instead of on wealth. I say that we have a perfect right to suggest that the tax should be placed upon wealth, and distributed fairly over the whole country. The mere fact of the war being on adds no weight to my hon. friend's argument.
The minister says that political considerations will not enter into the administration of the Act. I venture to say that if the terms of the Bill are the same as the terms of the resolution, the minister is taking into his hands vast power. He is taking power to nose into the private business of every concern of this country whose business comes within the scope of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would not that be the case if we adopted an income tax on individuals and companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I said in answer to the hon. member for Assiniboia was that the proceeds from the sale of stamps go into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the Dominion.	.

Through the Post
Office Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They go into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, no doubt through the Post Office Department.

I quite understand
'the point my hon. friend is making. My hon. friend knew quite well when he was making his statement that he was not meeting the point raised by my hon. friend from Assiniboia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He was.

Did not the people of this country last year think, when they were buying that additional stamp that went on to every letter and post card they mailed, that they were contributing to the Dominion treasury something that was to be ear-marked as a special-tax and which was to go into the fund that was to be devoted to carrying on the war?
Why did they mark it " war tax?"	)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was precisely what was d-one. The proceeds of the entire special war taxation went int-o Consolidated Revenue Fund, and out of that fund we paid for the purposes of the war very much more than was received from the special and the general taxation.
Is the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is only quibbling.

It is my hon. friend who is quibbling, and he knows it, because he knows that, if, in making that statement, he had said that the proceeds had gone into the Consolidated Revenue Fund through the Post Office, his statement would have been correct, I venture to state that the money that was received from the sale of those war stamps was not ear-marked and went into the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I consider my hon. friend's statement a mere quibble, and he knows it. There was never any intention of specially ear-marking any fund.
Sir WILFRID LtAURIER: Then, you did not ear-mark it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the financial system of this Dominion all' revenues, without any exception, even trust moneys go into Consolidated Revenue Fund. There is only one pocket that the Dominion has, and the point that T make is that last year we paid out of Consolidated Revenue Fund, into which the special and general taxation went, more for war expenditure than we derived from the special and general taxation, and I say that my hon. friend knows it.
I say further-and my hon. friend cannot contradict me-that he paid out to the Post Office Department $3,000,000 more than he got from it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the point.

My hon. friend is a quibbler-let there be no mistake about that. My hon. friend speaks about the Consolidated Revenue Fund of this country. He receives from certain departments of this Government certain amounts. He pays out certain amounts. The net amount which he receives from the Post Office Depart-
ment, or from the Railway Department, or from the Customs Department, or from any of the other departments in any particular year, is the amount which each particular department has by way of surplus from its administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is not.

I beg my hon.
friend's pardon. The revenue of the Post Office Department for last year was $13,-
026,000,	and the expenditure was $15,969,000. The money from the sale of those postage stamps, which were intended as a war tax, which should have been ear-marked as a war tax and kept for war purposes, was not so kept, but it went into the Post Office Department, and was absorbed in the general administration of that department, and the department costs more to administer than what it receives from all purposes, including the war tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the date of the Auditor General's Report from which my hon. friend is quoting?
I am quoting from the last one that has been laid on the table.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What date is it?
For the year ended March 31, 1915.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And my hon.
friend knows that the special taxation did not come into force until April 15, 1915.
Will my hon. friend say-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman want to quibble about that
again?

I was quoting that simply for illustration. I want to ask my hon. friend a question: Will my hon. friend say that the proceeds from the sale of those war stamps in 1915 have not gone into the revenue of the Post Office Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Your hon. friend will only say that my hon. friend has said more than enough for his own good.
That is my hon. friend's ultimatum. My hon. friend has been indulging in the worst kind of quibbling in which I have ever seen any minister indulge.
Oh, oh.
Hon. members laugh. I dare my hon. friend to deny that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are caught with the goods.

Well, my hon. friend is caught in deceiving this House, and I
say so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must say to the hon. member that his remark is quite out of order-
Not at all.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -that the hon. minister is deceiving the House. I would respectfully ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw the remark. I think on reflection he will agree with me that it is unparliamentary.	.

Well, in deference to you, Sir, I will substitute this statement, that the attitude of my hon. friend has the' effect of deceiving the House and the country. I make this statement in the committee in the presence of the Minister of Finance, that my hon. friend, instead of appropriating the money received from the war taxes imposed by means of the postage stamps that have been sold throughout the country since the imposition of the tax for war purposes, has allowed it to go into the general revenue of the Post Office Department, where it has been absorbed, and 1 state that that department has been run at a loss; that instead of economy being practised, the grossest kind of extravagance has been indulged in, and that as the people of this country will realize, my hon. friend has permitted this money, which was collected for war purposes, to be diverted by the Postmaster General to the general business of the Post Office Department. That is the statement I make, and the minister can not controvert it. He can quibble as he pleases with regard to it, but he cannot deny it. I wanted to make that as clear as possible.
Some hon. MEMBERS : ~Oh, oh.

If the Minister of
Finance contradicts that statement, I would be glad to give way to him that he may speak now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not like continually to interrupt my hon. friend. I say that his statement is entirely unfounded-a quibble; and, having regard to the intelligence I know he possesses, I cannot believe
but that he knows it to be a quibble. But if he says he does not know it, I withdraw that expression. When he concludes his re* marks, I shall be glad to give an expression to my views.
I am not asking for an expression of the hon. minister's views;: I am asking simply whether this tax is ear-marked for the purposes of the war, or whether he allows it to go into the general revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be glad
to deal with that.

And I shall be glad to hear my hon. friend. But I hope he will not deal in generalities about the money going into the consolidated revenue fund. We all know that all the revenues of Canada go into the consolidated fund. But we know also that in the case of the Government railways, for instance, the receipts are used to pay expenses, and only the balance of receipts over expenses, if there is such a balance, goes into the consolidated revenue of Canada at the end of the year. If there is no such surplus, nothing is added to the consolidated revenue fund. Now, as to the Post Office Department, the proceeds of the war tax were collected by the Post Office, and if there is no surplus in that department, the consolidated revenue fund does not get the money. So, my hon. friend cannot say that the money was devoted to war purposes. My statement is absolutely clear, and if he can controvert it he is welcome to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly can.

We will await the
hon. gentleman's statement. We were discussing the question of whether this Budget would work injury to the mining industry. My hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Green) very frankly tells us of the injury which he conceives these taxes will work to the mining industry of his province.
I spoke of the taxes as brought down. [DOT]

I was not going to misrepresent my hon. friend. When this Budget was brought down he thought that it would work great injury to the mining industry. But he says that, as a result of the amendments which have been made in' regard to operating mines, there would be no injury. And he says that
5 p.m. the companies of his province will not complain because they are asked to contribute something by way

of tax to carry on the war. But 'he cannot claim that the effect of these taxes will not be injurious so far as the prospector is concerned, the man who seeks to get capital into a mining venture.
I do not think the Budget affects the prospector.

The hon. gentleman means that there is no tax levied upon the man, but that the taxation is confined to companies. But he knows that, as regards the future company, it will place difficulties in the way of the man who has to look for capital to work a mining claim which he believes to be good.

If the hon. gentleman wants to represent my view, it is, as I said, that when this Budget came down I thought it would be injurious. I interviewed the Minister of Finance on the matter. But, with the amendment, and, with t'he explanation made by the minister, my opinion is that it will not injure the mining industry, nor will it place difficulties in the way of enfisting new capital in mining.

The hon. gentleman may be satisfied as regards existing companies, but he must appreciate the fact that the party who goes looking for capital to establish a mine will have to make a great many explanations to prospective investors before he can induce them to invest. We come back to the difficulty which underlies this whole proposition, the inability of my hon. friend, whether he be Minister of Finance or anything else, to give any guarantee to capital that this tax will not last longer than two years. We arg at a disadvantage in considering this question, because the Minister of Finance has not laid before the House a statement of the real commitments of this country in this war at the present time. We have dealt with generalities as to the expenditure of hundreds of millions, but we ought to know what we are spending day by day. Only with such information before us can the House and the country know whether or not this tax will be only temporary. Does the Minister of Finance mean to say that if it is necessary for him to continue this taxation after two years he will cut	off this	method of	taxation
and revert to some other method? If my hon. 'friends means to take that position and say that if we need taxation in this country we will not pursue the method we are now pursuing, after the 
end of two years, then you have some finality upon the question. But I did not understand my hon. friend to say that. He leaves it quite open, to himself, if the necessities of the country, in his judgment, require it, and if he is still in office, to pursue this method of taxation or any other method that seems good to him Hence the apprehension which many of us felt when this Budget was brought down that the possible investor outside of this country might feel, in fact, undoubtedly will feel, that a tax is being imposed in Canada which may be increased and which may have the effect of rendering wholly uncertain the returns upon such a speculative industry as mining necessarily is.

My hon.
friend has just given expression to some views which to me are very interesting. I do not agree with him, however, witli regard to difficulty in getting money for mines ini this country. I have no doubt that the Minister of Finance would be glad, if he were able to do so, to announce that zhere would be some finality to this1 tax. How can the Minister of Finance, or the Prime Minister, or any other member of the Government, or the hon. member for Pietou, say when finality will come to this war tax? No one knows when the finality of these taxes will come, and so long as we are at war no one expects a cessation of these taxes. We cannot be at war without raising money, and there is only one way a Government can raise money, that is, by taxation.
My hon. friend raises the question of getting money for mines. I represent a mining community, and it may be interesting to this committee to know that the mining industry is the second greatest industry in Canada. It may be interesting to 'this committee to know also that the mining industry produces more tonnage for our railways than any other industry in Canada; in fact, that it produces more 'tonnage for railways than all other industries in Canada combined. I have in my hand a statement which is compiled' by the United States Interstate Commerce Commission for the period from 1900 to 1906.

Does that statement
cover gross tonnage or ton miles?
It is the tonnage that originates as the product of mines.
That is gross.

I am not referring to the mile tonnage, but to the actual tonnage which exists and which the different railways haul. I find in this statement that the products of mines represent 52 'per cent of the total tonnage hauled by the railroads of the United States during these 6 years. A similar compilation with regard to the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, which, by the way, is the report I am quoting from, gives a similar statement; but the percentage is not quite so high-not quite 50 per cent, so far as that particular railroad is concerned. The point I desire to make is that in legislating for Canada no Government can afford to overlook the question of our mining industry, because of its tremendous importance.
To revert to the remarks of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), we very often have to go abroad for money to deveilop our mines. But let me ask him to what country we can go to-day for money to develop our mines where there are not war taxes. Can we go to Britain? The British Government does not permit money to leave Britain to-day for the development of mines in Canada. Can we go to France? There are war taxes in France. Can we go to Russia? There are war taxes in Russia. Can we go to Italy? There are war taxes in Italy. We do not want German money or Austrian money or Turkish money. Where else shall we go? To the United States? Are there no war taxes there? Six months before we put a war tax in this country, when we weTe at war, the United States put a wa. tax on-and they are not at war. -That war tax is still in existence. They have an income tax there. Therefore my hon. friend's argument falls to the ground, because you cannot go to the United States to get money for investment in mines if you are to go to a country that Jhas no war tax. So far as I am concerned and so far as that portion of this great industry with which I have some connection is concerned, there is no great fear about these taxes. So far as the mining industry and mining men in this country are concerned, they are as loyal, we are as loyal, as the hon. member for Pictou; they are prepared to pay their full share of these war taxes, and glad to do it.
I take exception to the proposition that the Guggenheimers of New York are as loyal to the British Empire as I am.

I have no doubt my hon. friend does take exception to it, because he has no knowledge of the facts. I dare say that the men who are interested in mining in this country, and the mine workers, are as loyal as my hon. friend from Pictou, and just as willing to contribute their share to this tax. There is no question about that. We are at war, we have to get the money to carry on the war, and it is to the Minister of Finance that the country looks to find the money. He proposes this tax; it is not unreasonable, and I know that the mining industry will be satisfied with it. Why, Mr. Chairman, two weeks ago, the body which speaks in Canada for the mining industry, the Canadian Mining Institute, met in this City of Ottawa, and I had the honour of introducing to the Minister of Finance a delegation from that body. They presented to him their views, and they assured him, in my presence, that they were willing and ready to contribute their full share of this taxation. The Mine Owners' Association of Ontario sent a delegation on the following day, and I had the honour of going with that delegation to the Minister of Finance. They presented the same views. We are at one on this question, and I repeat, the mining industry is quite willing, able, and glad to pay its full share of taxation necessary to carry on this great war.
I do not agree with my hon. friend from Pictou when he says that because of this tax we shall not be able to get capital to develop our mines. It is not the investor who is hit; it is only those companies that are _ making big profits from the advanced prices of materials, which are largely caused by the war, that will be hit. These are the companies that are going to be taxed, and these only. The men making small profits will not contribute. I submit that the mining industry will not be affected more than any other industry. I represent a class of mining that is different from any other section of that industry.	We all know
that mines have a limited life. Coal mines have perhaps the longest life, nickel perhaps next, copper next, silver, I fancy, next, gold perhaps next, but the shortest life of all is that pf placer mining, which is the chief industry in the territory 1 represent. This was one of the questions which the gentlemen who represented the Mining Institute submitted to the Minister of Finance,	and it is

a question of prime importance. The answer of my hon. friend was of great importance to that industry, and the answer he gave satisfied them that he was going to deal with their industry in a fair and equitable way by recognizing the principle which underlies it. He recognized that he was dealing with an industry different from agriculture, railways, lumbering, or any other branch of industry the products of which can be reproduced. But metal once taken from the soil cannot be reproduced. The Minister of Finance recognized that basic principle and assured the delegation that in casting his Bill he would proceed on the principle that a percentage of the capital in the industry is being taken yearly and distributed in profits, if profits are made. That answer satisfied those gentlemen, and I submit it was a fair and reasonable answer. That is why the mining industry will accept this Bill, and will be ready and willing to pay their full share of the ta/x.

The explanation given by my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Thompson) puts this proposal of the Finance Minister in a light which I certainly never understood before. Is the committee to understand that the Finance Minister is being granted power under this Bill to fix, according to his own judgment, and without any control on the part of this parliament, the limit of taxation that a mining company shall pay. If that be the fact, it opens up a most startling situation. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance is a man of the very best intentions, and I would cei'tainly trust him to do what was right in such a case, as' much as I would any other man in Canada. But the Minister of Finance to-day may not be the Minister of Finance to-morrow, and, in any case, this Parliament has a responsibility to the people and to the interests of this country which it cannot discharge by simply saying: we depend on the Minister of Finance. If that is the character of this legislation, it certainly has an application which I for. one never suspected. I thought it very questionable before, but it is certainly very much more questionable now. My hon. friend from the Yukon said that placer mining was a great source of wealth in that country. He said that the proposition now before the House would not adversely affect the mining interest. I suppose he was speaking particularly of the Yukon, Mining in the Yukon to-day is being carried on as the result of

an enormous investment of capital, I do not know just how many millions are represented in that investment, but I suppose it would be. perhaps $10,000,000.
About twice that.
About.

I am speaking of one
company-the Yukon Gold Company?
Of that company only?
