We will, for the purposes of my argument, assume that the Yukon Gold Company has made an investment of $10,000,000 for the purpose of producing placer gold in the Yukon. Necessarily, the life of a placer gold mine in the Yukon, as it must be everywhere else, is limited. I am not sure that the men who invested their money in that gold field knew what the life of the field was going to be when the investment was made. I do not know that that is known yet. I think it would be proper to say that it is absolutely not known yet. If the men who invested their money in that Yukon gold company's enterprise had had to face taxation legislation of this character, in which it was left, as I understand, absolutely in the hands of the Minister of Finance as to whether they should pay a larger or a smaller rate of taxation; as to whether they might be taxed out of business within a certain period of years, I am here to say that the money would never have been invested. There is no argument on that subject; it would never have been invested under those circumstances and with that prospect in view.
Does the hon. gentleman say that there is any discrimination involved in this resolution?

I do not say there is any discrimination involved in the resolution, and that is what surprises me. There is certainly discrimination proposed, under the explanation as given by the member for Yukon. He tells the House that it is proposed to leave in the hands of the minister the absolute right to vary the taxation on mining properties according to his best judgment. I know that such a proposal must have a most serious effect in preventing the investment of capital in the development of mining in Canada.
Is that the text of the resolution?	,

No, it is not the text of the resolution; but the House has been informed by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Green), and by the hon. member for Yukon, both gentlemen representing mining constituencies, that the minister has explained, that this is to be the course taken. I am taking their explanation, as they have given it, I suppose, in perfectly good fait'h, and I am very much surprised and alarmed at the nature of the explanation. I would hope that it is not correct, and that the minister does not propose to assume any such unlimited measure of authority in dealing with a question that is so important as the taxation of mining properties. This is a different question from that of the taxation of other business enterprises, because the profits of a mining property exhaust the capital year by year, while the profits of any other enterprise djO not exhaust capital in the same way.
Speaking of the proposal as a whole, if I understood the minister correctly, he said that this proposal was strictly a war measure to meet war conditions. Therefore I would assume that it is a temporary measure of taxation not intended to be continued indefinitely when war conditions have ceased. If I am correct in that, and I believe I am, I would take the opportunity of putting this view before the committee. We are not expecting or proposing by this measure of taxation, or any other measure of taxation that we are putting in force, to pay the capital charges of the war. We are only proposing to provide for the necessary interest charges. These interest charges are not a matter of the continuance of the war; they are a matter of the period of the loan whidh is raised in order to provide for the war during its continuance. Any provision that only contemplates providing for the interest charges for a short period, or during the continuance of the war, is certainly inadequate. We must face the condition that we have when we have incurred a capital obligation of $300,000,000, $400,000,000, of $&00,000,000, and interest on that capital obligation must be met for at any rate, we will say, a period of thirty years. It seems to me it would have been the part of wisdom for the minister, in preparing this scheme of taxation, to have prepared a scheme that would be suitable and, would be available permanently for meeting these interest charges. It is most unfortunate if we are to have a temporary scheme of taxation imposed which admittedly has so many drawbacks
and difficulties to overcome when we have to meet a permanent condition. We should meet that permanent condition by permanent preparation, and not by temporary preparation. My understanding of the position of the minister is that he recognizes that this proposal is not a suitable proposal as a permanent means of raising interest on war loans. Is it because he realizes that this is a tax upon enterprise rather than upon wealth, and that, inasmuch as it is a tax upon enterprise it cannot be successfully maintained during the period of the war loan, while putting an obstacle in the way of the expansion of the industrial and commercial interests of the country?
If I remember correctly, the Minister of Finance, when introducing this measure, laid stress upon the excessive profits of munition contractors, the munition contracts being a war condition. Everybody will agree that a temporary measure, to apply to the excessive profits of munition contractors, would be fair and reasonable. Not to criticise or find1 fault with the gentlemen engaged on munition contracts, the fact undoubtedly remains that while the business of the country at large is not in a buoyant condition, their business is in a particularly buoyant condition. They are in a position to pay a considerable share of the taxation, and their profits will cease when the war ceases. It is, therefore, reasonable that provision should be made for taxation of war profits as a war measure. That is easily understood, which cannot be said for a scheme of taxation that applies to all business, and is only temporarily a war measure; for general business in some form or another will have to carry the permanent liability resulting from our war obligations.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Thompson) mentioned that the United States have adopted income taxation as a war measure. That is a tax on wealth, and chiefly on accumulated wealth. Now, that is a permanent proposition. It stands to-day, tomorrow, and as long as the taxation is needed. It seems to me that a taxation measure, not necessarily on the exact line followed in the United States, but on the principle of laying down a system which would be as permanent as our war obligations, and which would be a tax on wealth rather than on industry or enterprise, is what would appeal most strongly to the people of this country, and would be more to the advantage of the country than the proposals made by the Minister of Finance.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the numerous arguments made toy hon. gentlemen opposite against these taxation proposals. I do not intend to speak at any great length; but one statement has been made which I feel I cannot let pass unchallenged. The hon. member for Pictou, for the second time in this debate, practically charged the Finance Minister with intentionally deceiving the House on the question of taxation, and he based his argument on the expenditure and revenue of the Post Office Department. The hon. member on a former occasion made use of these' words:
The hon. Finance Minister last year, in the most solemn tones that he could command, asked for the imposition of an additional tax of one cent on every letter that went through the mails of this country, for the purpose, forsooth, of meeting war expenditure. Taxes upon patent medicines and upon various things were included, the minister saying that the people should willingly accept the imposition of this taxation in order that we might thereby provide the funds to pay the interest upon the debt that we were contracting in order to fight the battles of old England. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the proceeds of not one of the stamps that were put upon letters in all parts of the country were devoted to war purposes. Every cent and every dollar made up from this source was appropriated by the Post Office Department for the purpose of paying the extra clerks in Montreal and Quebec, and of meeting the boundless run of extravagance that was begun by Hon. Mr. Pelletier, and that is being ..continued by the present Postmaster General.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says,
"hear, hear." He took up a blue-book and was endeavouring to lead the House to believe that there was a deficit in the Post Office Department this year of at least $3,000,000, when the Finance Minister forced him to acknowledge that he was Teading from practically an ancient report, or at least not from a report of the revenue and expenditures for this year; and my hon. friend went on to make a bitter and unjustifiable attack on &>e Finance Minister. Now, I wish to give the House the actual figures of the revenue and expenditures of the Post Office Department since this tax of an extra cent was imposed in April last. For the nine months from April to December of the year 1915, the revenue of the Post Office Department was $14,019,874, and the expenditure $11,705,370: that is there was a surplus for the nine months ol $2,314,504. I submit that in view of these figures, which the hon. member for Pictou cannot deny, he owes an apology to this v

House and to the Minister of Finance for the reckless and unjustifiable statement he made. The figures show that there will be a surplus of $3,250,000 for the Post Office Department this year, and that will go to assist in the prosecution of the war. The hon. member for Pictou knows perfectly well that under the system of financing we have in this country the total revenues go into Consolidated Fund, and the surplus from that fund is now being used for the prosecution of the war. Certainly now is not the time to suggest that we should have a new system of financing, or that we should ear-mark every dollar from this source and that so as to be sure that it is used for war purposes. Why, in order to keep track of every dollar and allocate it to this or that fund, we should have to double the staff of the various departments.
You could not find places for them.
My hon. friend's mind is running back to the time when he was sitting behind the treasury benches.
I meant that you could not find sitting room in the departments.
I do not think my hon. friend's remark is very pertinent.
The hon. member for Pictou was endeavouring to estimate the net result of the financial operations of the Post Office Department for the present fiscal year.
And he made a pretty poor fist of it.

He was urging a more economical administration of that department, and contending that if. the department were economically managed it would at least pay for itself, and would not eat up the revenue which the Government was obtaining from wiar stamps. Will the hon. gentleman tell me what he estimates the deficit of the Post Office Department will be for the year ending on the last of this month, not crediting to the Post Office Department the revenue from the war stamps?
I will answer that in a minute. My hon. friend says-and I am surprised at the hon. member for Pictou being suddenly struck dumb, as he usually has the last word.
My hon. friend will hear from me at the proper time.
I am glad that my hon. friend has found his tongue again.
They can, not both speak at the same time.

My hon. friend says: "I was endeavouring to show what the deficit is this year." He can figure and he can produce blue-books by the ton, but he will not be able to show what the deficit is this year; he will find a surplus in nine months *of $2,314,504.
But that is counting war-tax revenue.
Certainly, and the tax was put on for war purposes.

That is not counting only the Post Offive revenue, but in-'[DOT]oluding revenue from other sources-. What is the result without the war-tax revenue?
. Mr. STEVENS: I will come to that in a >second. Let me lay down this as a fundamental principle - and the Postmaster 'General in the former Government and the Tight hon. leader of the Opposition will [DOT]agree with me-that the Post Office Department is not supposed to be a revenue-producing department.
It used to be.
Not with the Tories in -oifiee.
Answer the question.

I will most assuredly answer the question. The policy originated by the right hon. gentleman now leading the Opposition, when Sir William Mulock was Postmaster General, and when they reduced the postage from three cents to two cents, w-as this: That they did not want the Post Office to be a revenue-producing department, but they wanted it simply to pay its way. In the year ended March 31, 1914, there was a deficit in the Post Office Department, but 75 or 80 per cent of the business concerns throughout Canada showed a deficit during the first few months after the war broke out., and the Post Office Department was probably affected in its revenue more severely than any other department.
The revenue of the Post Office Department did not fall off. My hon. friend is not answering my question.

If my hon. friend will not be patient until I come to his question, I
will answer it now, even although it makes my remarks disjointed. My hon. friend asks why there was a deficit in the Post Office Department? I say: because the Government carried out one of the most important planks in its platform, namely, the extension of rural mail deliveries throughout this country plus the parcel post system. Will the hon. .gentleman or his leader take the responsibility of condemning here the policy of the Government in extending rural mail deliveries?
It is not necessary,

He certainly will not, and no sane man will condemn it. But my hon. friends from Halifax and Pictou are condemning the Government, and indirectly placing themselves in the position of condemning rural mail delivery and increased postal facilities. I will give my hon. friend an illustration right in my own district.
My hon. friend is not answering my question. He was going to do so a minute or two ago.
I am answering it as fast as I can.
He will forget about it soon.

My hon. friend keeps on interrupting with new questions. Let us take the revenue and expenditure of this year. I show here by official figures from the accountant of the Post Office Department, that in nine months we have a surplus of $2,314,504.
Including the war stamp taxation.
Certainly including the war stamp taxation, and this surplus is going to assist in financing the war, just as the Minister of Finance told the House a year ago.
What would be the result excluding the war stamp tax?

Judging from the amount of the war stamp tax, I should say, although I have not the figures before me, that the Post Office Department will come out even, and that is exactly the policy which the right hon. gentleman followed for years and which this House is not prepared to turn down, namely, that the Post Office Department shall break even. '
There will be a deficit of from three to five million dollars in that department.

Then there is all the
more credit to the Minister of Finance for his financing. My hon. friend has not at all succeeded in getting over the malicious attack of the hon. member for Pictou on the Minister of Finance when he stated that the minister had a deficit in the Post Office Department, and that he was deceiving the House and the country. The Minister of Finance has, by his method of financing, succeeded in producing a surplus which is being devoted to the prosecution of this war, and a few dollars here or there are not particularly concerning my hon. friends opposite. I repeat that, so far as the increased expenditure is concerned, you have the parcel post, rural mail delivery, and increased postal facilities throughout the Dominion.

Over $4,000 in the
county of the hon. member for Pictou.

The hon. member said: " Why did the minister not put on an income tax?" Two or three years ago my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and my hon. friend 'from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and others raged in this House about the trusts, mergers, and combines, about this industrial concern and that industrial concern, as if they had no right to exist in the country. Now they say: "Why does the Minister of Finance tax the industries of the country? why does he not leave those industries free?" Yet many of them are making huge profits out of war expenditures at the present time. They know this, if they know anything, that the people of Canada welcome the proposal of the Minister of Finance as a most radical advance in the system of taxation. The minister has cut the ground from under the feet of my hon. friends opposite, and that is what causes them so much anxiety, because it gives them mighty little to condemn this Government for on the hustings. The people are behind the Government. I would like my hon. friend from Edmonton and my hon. friend from Pictou to stand before the labour element in their constituencies and condemn this Government for the taxation proposals contained in this measure. They will go in a nice, quiet, gentlemanly fashion to the captains of industry and say to them: "You poor fellows; you are paying all this taxation; why do you not get after this nefarious and socialistic Government and put it out of business?" Then when they come to the working men, they will forget to say: " Why did you not ask for an income tax?"
My hon. friend spoke about a white British Columbia some time ago.

My hon. friend will, at least, say that I have been consistent in my opinions. I have a deep regard for the hon. gentleman's leader, yet the right hon. gentleman has not been quite so consistent, perhaps, as I have been in regard to a white British Columbia. In British Col-umbit he was in favour of it, but down here for fifteen years he drifted, with not very much done, except to disallow 144 Acts of the British Columbia Legislature. If the hon. member for Pictou or the right hon. leader of the Opposition desires to fight out the question of a white British Columbia in British Columbia, taking the stand the hon. gentleman suggests at the present time, I am quite satisfied.
Now, let us have a word as to the income tax. These hon. gentlemen know perfectly well that there is not a province in Canada that does not impose an income tax. This is a system of taxation which is peculiarly adapted to the provinces, and it has always been considered inadvisable for the Dominion Government to invade that field of taxation. I venture the suggestion that these hon. gentlemen would not dare to include that as a definite plank in their platform. My hon. friend says that this system is not permanent. If our present methods of taxation do not bring the result desired, we may have to resort to many other forms. But the system introduced by the Finance Minister last year has been a splendid success, and we know that the system introduced this year has been accepted throughout the length and breadth of the country, and it also will be a success. But if the war continues and the expenditure increases, and if the people of Canada must bear a larger burden of taxation, I think they will be prepared to bear it cheerfully.
I desired to speak on the mining aspect of this question, but I will refrain, except, to make one observation with regard to copper, which may be of some interest. I do not know that this is exactly time to introduce this suggestion, but I do not know of a better. Last year, in discussing the Budget, I strongly advocated the refining of copper in Canada. 1 understand that the Government has given the .matter a great deal of attention, and with such success that a copper refinery will be established. To strengthen this idea, let me give a few

figures. Last year, we exported from Canada
221,000,000 pounds of copper. As I understand it, our copper is exported mainly in the form of matte. On the other hand, we imported 115,000,000 pounds of copper- about half the amount of our export. Here is the point to which I would draw the attention of the Government and the House. For the 220,000,000 pounds of copper that we exported, we received $25,000,000; but for the 115,000,000 we imported we paid $19,000,000. In other words we exported copper at 11J cents and imported copper at 161 cents. That should emphasize the necessity of having copper refineries within our own borders sufficient to supply all Canada. It is poor business to sell copper at 11| cents and to import copper-a great deal of it re-imported-at 16S cents.	,	[DOT]

The hon. gentleman
<Mr; Stevens) congratulates the Government on having arranged for the refining of copper in Canada. What has the Government done to bring about this condition?

I do not think it is my place to deal with that. I leave that to the Finance Minister. I pressed this matter upon the attention of the Government last year, and others have done the same. The intimation is conveyed to me from other sources that steps in the matter have already been taken. Certain gentlemen wrote to me asking for information which I gladly supplied, but that was a private matter, and I do not think it would interest the House.

My hon. friend, rushing to the defence of the Minister of Finance, charges me with maliciously attacking that hon. gentleman. I plead not guilty to the charge of malice. I admit that I spoke with some vigour. But if it is necessary, in order to make clear our views on this side of the House, to speak with vigour, I hope the hon. gentleman will not take that as indicating any malicious feeling. Coming to the rescue of the Finance Minister, he produces from somewhere-and in view of all the circumstances one might be pardoned for doubting the authenticity of his figures, a statement the effect of which was to show that the money collected by the post office as war tax did not go to the financing of the war, but went to pay expenses of the Post Office Department. He showed that for nine months' operations, including the money that came from the war tax, there would be a surplus of $2,300,000. In other words,
taking the revenues from ordinary sources and add,ing the revenues that came from the sale of w^ar-tax stamps, you get an amount, which, when all credited to the post office, amounts to $2,300,000 more than the expenses' of that department. This proves exactly what I have said-that this money went to the Post Office Department and not to pay war expenses. Then the hon. gentleman said, a little disingenuously it seemed to me, that the policy of all governments was not to have a surplus in the Post Office Department. Well, turning to this report, I find that from 1903 down to 1911, under the administration of my right hon. leader there was a surplus every year, the lowest being $400,000 and the highest $1,100,000.

But what is-
'Mr. MACDONALD: My hon. friend is usually dreaming about something in the clouds, or something thousands of years or thousands of miles away, and wants to ask a question about it. I do not mind answering a question that relates to the subject.
The hon. gentleman himself is not backward in asking questions.

I have shown surpluses under the Liberal Government. Now, take the policy of this Government down to 1915. In 1911 there was a surplus of $1,100,000; in 1913, $1,800,000; in 1914, $1,177,000. So, the policy of both Governments was to have a substantial surplus in the Post Office Department. As a result of the administration of somebody, they now have a deficit of $3,000,000. The hon. member for Vancouver says we have a surplus of $2,300,000, with all the returns not in. these additional war tax stamps would be $7,000,000.

Has my hon. friend eliminated from that calculation all the 5 cent stamps, the registry stamps, and the 1 cent stamps? Are his figures for 2 cent stamps alone? Has he eliminated the parcel post -and the newspaper fees which are paid in bulk?
As my hon. friend, who came here to give information for the Government, failed to give information on the vital point, we can only take the figures here and make an approximation.
There should be a certain reduction.
Suppose we strike off
Strike off one-half.

Not at all; I do not assent to that. But suppose we say that $5,000,000 was obtained 'as the result of the sale of this additional 1 cent stamp, then the Post Office Department' got at least $4,000,000 in the period my hon. friend has mentioned from the sale of war-tax stamps, and they are including that in their $2,000,000 surplus. The result is that if we cut out of their figures the $4,000,000, which they got from the war-tax stamp, there would be a deficit at the end of nine months of $1,700,000, instead of a surplus of $2,300,000. The result of all this goes to show that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, instead of taking this money, which the people of Canada paid on the supposition that they were paying it for war purposes, and appropriating it for war fund account, as he should have done, permits the Post Office Department to treat it just the same as the revenue from any other stamps sold in the post office and absorb it into their fund and charge it up in their account; and if there is no surplus in the Post Office Department on the 31st of March, my hon. friend gets nothing for the war.
Yes, but there is a surplus.

My hon. friend does not know whether there is going to be a surplus. He has some figures, but not all of the figures. We are told that there was a surplus of $2,300,000 in the Post Office Department for the nine months, including the 
war tax, the amount of which my hon. friend cannot tell us. If $4,000,000 was derived from the sale of war tax stamps, then in that particular year they derived their surplus from the sale of the war stamps.-Had it not been for this additional revenue-there would have been a deficit of $1,700,-000-and all the returns are not in yet. All my hon. friend has done is to prove exactly the statement I made. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, instead of getting a large revenue from the sale of war tax stamps, is not going -to get a cent; it will' all be absorbed by the Post Office Department, and instead of going to pay interest on the debt, as the people of Canada were led to believe, it is being appropriated by the Postmaster General to run the Post Office Department.

Why do you not back
up your statements with facts?
My hon. friend has wakened up again. He is usually dreaming-about
No, it was only a nightmare.

My hon. friend has one of these nightmare spells of his every once in a while. My hon. friend has been sleeping so far, he has not followed me when I have shown that the Minister of Finance has allowed the Postmaster General to take away the money derived from the sale of war tax stamps, instead of leaving it in a fund where he could use it to pay the interest on the war loans. The Minister of Finance knows it, and the House knows it. My hon. friend does not want to bear the onus of this situation. I can quite understand that he would not; but there is the fact, and it is useless to deny it.
I wish to refer to a suggestion the hon. member from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) made 'with reference to -the attitude of hon. members on this side of the House towards labour. My hon. friend is the last member in this House who should talk about labour. So long as the Liberals were in power, he denounced the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid' Laurier) to the labour men for having vetoed the fake legislation that he and his Conservative friends were passing in the Provincial Legislature. The moment, responsibility came, my hon. friend evidently forgot all about a white British Columbia. But the labour men of British

My hon. friend raised
the question; I did not.

I said nothing
about the labour question.

this side have no fear of a comparison of records in regard to the treatment oi the subjects of the great nation which is one of the most valued allies of the British Empire in this war.

speechtext: A word in regard to what my hon. friend from Pictou (*Mr. Macdonald) has said. He seems to have a remarkable idea of the operations of the Post Office Department, or any other department -of this Government Apparently, as far as I understand his argument, he imagines that when the Post Office Department has a surplus of $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 or $300,000,000 at the end of a year, it takes that and locks it up in the safe, and appropriates it the next year for the purposes of its expenditure.

I took an entirely
different view, and my right hon. friend must know it. I said it was the Minister of Finance, because he gets the surplus.
bir ROBERT BORDEN:	All I have to
say is that if my hon. friend did not mean that, he meant nothing; because the Minister of Finance has stated over and over again, and every one in the House except my hon. friend knows it, that when .there is a surplus in any department of Government, that surplus goes into the consolidated revenue fund and
I said so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I said so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

Then, if he said that, he argued precisely the opposite to that, because he declared that this surplus was to be used for the Post Office Department and for nothing else, and was retained

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I suggest that you read clause 17, then, Mr. Chairman.
On section 17-restriction as to line in Prince Rupert and in certain provinces:

I observe that section 17, which is intended as a saving clause, covers the point that has reference to Alberta, in so far as the construction of new lines is concerned; but it does not cover the point of the acquiring of existing lines or rights in other provinces. I think that is important.
The words "operate and maintain" would cover that.

I do not think so, because these words are subject to the word "construct." That is the only question I wish to raise in regard to the Bill, and, if it is agreed on the part of the promoters to accept that principle, I would ask that the

point be made definite in this particular section.

I think this clause would cover it. They could not operate a line in other provinces without first procuring the consent of the legislatures, and, not having the power to operate, there would be no use of purchasing a line in those provinces. Whether it covers the point or not, it was discussed very fully in committee, and the committee decided that the clause did cover the point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton.

I would be inclined to disagree. I think that the words "operate or maintain " are subject to the word "construct," and it would be so construed. There would be no harm done by making the provision that I suggest. I respectfully suggest that such an amendment be made.
There would be no objection to covering the point mentioned by my hon. friend.

While the Provincial
Government of Alberta owns and operates a provincial telephone system, the city of Edmonton has a system of its own, which it had established before the province undertook the operation of telephones. There are also other private enterprises occupying territory that the Government has not yet entered upon. It is not desirable that this territory should be occupied by an outside telephone company except with the consent of the Government of Alberta.

The counsel had that matter before him, and he understands that it is fully covered by this clause. If this company proposed to purchase in the province of Alberta or the province of Saskatchewan any line which is now in-operation, they would have to do it subject to this Bill, and the Bill would not allow them to operate the line without first obtaining the consent of the Government. Therefore, it would be useless for them to purchase a line in Saskatchewan or Alberta unless they had the right to operate it.

I may be wrong, but my
reading of the Bill is that it provides that they shall not operate or maintain the line they have constructed, but it does not provide that they shall not operate and maintain the line they have purchased.

There is no objection on
the part of the promoters of the Bill to have that covered if my hon. friend thinks it is necessary.

This clause was inserted at the request Of the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Douglas), with exactly the object in view that my hon. friend has, to his entire satisfaction and to the satisfaction of the counsel of the committee, and it was accepted by the promoters of the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think that the words will bear the meaning which my hon. friend from Edmonton puts upon them. They are in the disjunctive-the company shall not construct, shall not operate, shall not maintain, any line of telephone without the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council in any of the provinces mentioned.

I am willing to accept the interpretation of the Prime Minister. There is, however, a further point in regard to section 17 that I wish to draw attention to. The concluding words are:
But this restriction shall not apply to the construction, operation or maintenance of long distance lines of the company into or through the said city of Prince Rupert or into or through any or all of the said provinces.
The latter words contemplate giving the company the right to construct a long-distance line across the province of Alberta without the consent of the Governor in Council. Now, they cannot construct a line across the province of Alberta with out either purchasing a right of way or occupying the road allowances. Therefore, I think it is only reasonable that when we empower them to build across the province of Alberta they should be subject to the consent of the Governor in Council, just as any other telephone line is that is constructed within the province. I do not see why a difference is made between a line that is carried completely across the province, and a line that is carried only into the province.

The object is not to empower the company to build across the province, but to allow them to connect up with the lines in the hon. gentleman's province. They are not looking for local business, but they want to connect their lines up and do a through business. If the hon. gentleman insists, I see no reason why we should not say, "'subject to the consent of the Governor in Council." The company is not seeking to construct any new lines, but simply to connect up with the lines already in the province.

I have no objection at all to the organization of the company, except
that when it comes inside the province of Alberta it must in some degree conflict with the conditions existing there. I think that as the principle is recognized in the remainder of the section, we might very well recognize it here by striking out all the words after " Prince Rupert Then they would have rights within the province subject to the Governor in Council, which is really all that the company requires.

I should like to point out that at almost every sitting of this House we pass Bills allowing railway companies to operate telephone lines over their systems, and through any provinces. This section specifically prevents the company from operating in Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Alberta without the consent of the Governor in Council. Surely there can be no objection to this company connecting up its lines for long-distance purposes. In the event of their getting consent from the province of Saskatchewan, what objection could there possibly be to their having communication between Saskatchewan and British Columbia, so long as the local business of the province of Alberta is thoroughly protected? We are giving this privilege to dozens of railway companies, and I cannot see any objection to giving it to this company. I think my hon. friend will agree that there has been little danger to the interests of the provinces.

The situation of a railway company is entirely different. No province is operating a monopoly railway system. Permission to construct a telephone line alongside a railroad is entirely different to permission to construct a telephone line alone. My suggestion was simply to strike out the words after " Prince Rupert. That would leave the matter where it ought to be, namely, that when the company goes into or crosses a province it is subject to the consent of the Governor in Council of that province.

Perhaps we had better let
the section stand for the moment.

The solicitor tells me that section 17 was inserted in the particular shape in which it is now at the express request of the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Douglas). It was his opinion that it would be wise to give the three provinces the power to construct long-distance lines. I understand that he is on his way here. As all the rest of the Bill has been put through the committee stage, I think we



had better let this section remain as it is, because the matter was discussed very thoroughly in the Railway Committee. If the bom member insists, rather than let the Bill stand, I will agree to have the section struck out; but, under the circum- . stances, I would like to have the Bill go through committee to-night, and, if there is any valid objection, we can deal with it later

I do not wish to delay the Bill at all, nor to d,eal lightly with the consideration given to it by the committee, but the greater part of this section clearly contemplates the consent of the Governor-in Council of any other province than British Columbia for the extension of telephone lines into that province. That is agreed?
Yes.

The last line, however, provides that the extension can be made without the consent of the Governor in Council. That is a contradiction in terms, and I may say that I feel very strongly on that point from the fact that the province of Alberta operates its own telephone lines, excepting in the city of Edmonton, which operates its telephone lines. I have been communicated with by the mayor of Edmonton in regard to this Bill. I do not wish to insist too much, but I would withdraw all opposition if the promoter would agree to out out the words after the words "Prince Rupert": "Or into or through any or all of the said provinces." That would leave the section carrying out its original intent, which I maintain is contradicted by the insertion of those words.

Would my hon. friend
accept this suggestion:	Let the Bill go
through committee and be reported, and let the third Teading stand until he has an opportunity to discuss this section with the hon. member for'Strathcona, and then before the third reading that amendment can be made if it is thought desirable. I think the hon. member is really making a mistake in pressing for the striking out of this section.
Mr. OLIVER. I would not feel justified in taking that course. It is as plain as print can make it that the last line of the section contradicts the first part. We want to carry out either the first intent or the last intent, and I certainly suggest that the first intent be carried out and that the words I have read be struck out.

I have no desire to press .
this section against the hon. gentleman s views; and, if he is not prepared to let the Bill pass through committee and be reported, and then make an amendment if necessary on the third reading, we will strike the words out now; but I would have preferred to have the Bill go through the, committee to-night.	,

In the committee is the
proper place to make changes of this character, and I would ask the promoter to make the change in the committee.
Perhaps it would be better* if we strike out anything at all, to strike out everything after the word " aforesaid," and thus cut out all the restriction part of the section.
I have no objection to that at all. I am not concerned in that.

I move, then:
That all the words after " aforesaid " in the tenth line of section IT be struck out.

and so on. Section 12 of the Bill provides:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Undoubtedly.
ivfr. CARVELL:	Would the minister
kindly explain the principle on which depreciation will be allowed in -the working [DOT]of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The principle
would be the usage in a particular business with respect to the matter of depreciation. My hon. friend, as a lawyer, will know precisely what I mean when I say that the question of depreciation is a question of fact. The depreciation may be more in the case of one class of business than in another; it depends entirely upon the facts of the case. It is obvious that if a business has a certain amount of apparent profits at the end of the year, and on the other hand, there has been an ascertainable depreciation in the value of the machinery or plant, that should be deducted in order that the true net profits might be arrived at. Of course, there are elements besides depreciation that enter into the question of net profits; the expenses of the business an4 interest upon borrowed money are elements as well as depreciation.

Borrowed money would not be depreciation. If I understand the minister, he proposes to ask the different companies which he imagines would come under the provisions of this Act to submit statements. We all know that companies keep their books in many different ways. Some companies might write off five per cent a year for depreciation; some might write off as much as ten per cent. Take a company like that, and,, perhaps, their books would show that their capital was all gone. Of course, it would not be gone, because they would have a valuable plant left. Reserves might be established and used for replenishing the plant. In that case they would take care of the depreciation. In other cases there might not have iMr. Doggie.]
been enough money around to provide for depreciation. As a matter of good busines, a sum should be set aside for depreciation, but often it is not. It may have been paid out in dividends. In a case like that, would the minister consider that the company was entitled to write off, or reserve, a reasonable amount for depreciation, considering the nature of the business, or would be take the statement as furnished, by the company, and the conditions under which the company has been carrying on its business or keeping its books. We know that there are some classes of business that would depreciate to a very much greater extent than others. Take the ordinary manufacturing establishment; probably the depreciation there would not be anything like so much as it would be,- say, in the case of public utility corporations. In the case of a telephone company, for example, the depreciation naturally would be very great, because there is a depreciation of pole lines and cross arms, while there is obsolescence of the telephone plant generally. New ideas are coming forward, new switch boards and things of that kind are being introduced. If you take a manufacturing concern, on the other hand, say the Dominion Iron and Steel Company-I am taking that as an illustration-there is not very much depreciation of the machinery for the making of steel rails or steel rods. If I have made myself clear, does the minister feel like laying down any general principles upon which this question of depreciation might be determined in estimatng the taxation payable by a company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I draw the attention of my hon. friend to section 5, subsection 3:
No deductions from gross profits for depreciation or for any expenditure of a capital nature for renewals, or for the development of a trade or business or otherwise, in respect to the trade or business, shall be allowed except such amount as appears to the minister to be reasonable.
That is the whole question : what does thg minister consider reasonable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This Act, like any other Act, will be administered by the officials of the Government, the minister of course being responsible as head of the department. No principle can be laid down except this: that depreciation must be considered in estimating the net profits. The question of what is a reasonable depreciation in connection with any business is a

matter to be determined, as the officials may be able to determine, according to good usage in businesses of that character. For example, it may be quite proper in connection with one business to allow 2 per cent or 5 per cent; in others the depreciation may be much larger. It depends entirely upon the character of the business and upon the depreciation which necessarily results from the operation of the machinery and plant. I do not believe that I can give any more definite information than that. My hon. friend knows that depreciation, as I have said, is a question of fact. It seems to me that it is no more difficult to determine what is reasonable depreciation than it is to determine the reasonable value of property. That is determined by assessors all over the country yearly in connection with municipal and other assessments.

Is that the principle
which the minister is now laying down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The principle
which I lay down is that thd depreciation must be considered to be fair to a business, but as to the precise percentage, I cannot say definitely, because that will depend upon the facts.

I think -that, probably,
that is the only answer the minister could give, although I thought that possibly he might have had in his mind some general rules which he could give to the committee, and through the committee to the country, so that companies and persons liable to be assessed all over Canada would have some would have some way of figuring out the matter for themselves, Take two businesses " of exactly the same kind; one plant would naturally depreciate to a much greater extent than the other, because it depends upon the degree of permanency with which the plant has been created in the beginning. You might have one plant that would be practically permanent, and another more or less temporary, yet producing the same result in the end. Of course, in the one case, there would be very much less depreciation than in the other. In any case where real depreciation could be shown as the ordinary result of carrying on the business, regardless of what the books showed would he take that into consideration in arriving at the net profits of the concern?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What we should * do is to call upon the companies, such as I think my hon. friend has in mind, for a
statement, and in that statement, no doubt, an allowance would be made for depreciation. If that appeared to be too great an amount, it would be within the power of the department to disallow it, and, possibly, to allow a lesser amount, In the first instance we would ask the company or firm to make a return. I fully appreciate my hon. friend's point. Let us take the case, say, of electrical machinery, or of machinery in connection with public utilities; it is subject to very considerable depreciation. Not only that, but the progress of invention has frequently to be taken into consideration. I do not believe I can lay down any general principle, except to say that it is a question of fact, to be determined upon the evidence before us at the time and upon the usage respecting the plants of industrial and other concerns. I think, for example, that a technical expert could inform the department as to what would be a reasonable amount to allow in connection with a certain class of business, or even a particular plant in that business. There might be a greater depreciation in connection with one individual business than in another individual business of the same class; but we would strive to act uniformly.
Mr. LOG-GIE: Would the department be
willing to accept the last balance sheet prepared by a firm from their books? I do not mean that this should apply to the future, but that it should be taken as evidence of the results of the last year's business. For example, a firm has been doing business in a certain way, and, when it prepares its balance sheet, it writes off what, in its judgment, is the proper amount, and presents its business in the true light to its bankers. If an established business, following its usual practice for years, had written off bad debts and depreciation and given a statement to its bankers, would such a statement for the last year's business be acceptable to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say that it would be conclusive evidence, but I would say that it would be prima facie' evidence, and in all probability such a statement would be accepted; but it would not do for me to say that it must be accepted, because there must be power in the department to say: " We do not agree with what has been done." But, in connection with such a business as my hon. friend has in view, I think I would be justified in saying that there would be a very strong probability of its being accepted.

Would my hon. friend
be kind enough to illustrate by example the exact meaning of subsection " c " of clause 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was brought
to our attention after these resolutions were laid before the House that many Canadian businesses, and many businesses such as British, French and Belgian loan companies operating in Canada, are obliged, under taxation measures in the United Kingdom, France, and Belgium, to pay very heavy war taxation in those countries, so much heavier than our war taxation that ours appears trifling by comparison.
Do not be too modest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a fact. I might tell my hon. friend exactly what was brought to my attention. The amounts which some Canadian companies, and some non-Canadian companies operating in Canada, are obliged to pay in the United Kingdom, France, and Belgium would surprise him. They certainly surprised me. It was felt that, as these companies are taxed in respect to their Canadian business, to add this tax to the taxes they already bear, and whose proceeds go to the same cause, would be to put an oppressive burden on them. Consequently, we thought it would be advisable to insert subsection " c."

How would you do in the case of 'a transportation company?
, Suppose the Canadian Northern, or the Canadian Pacific, or any such transportation company having head offices in Montreal, Quebec, St. John, or Halifax, and coming under this measure and having offices in the United Kingdom, France or Italy, were hit there also, how would you arrive at the difference in the amounts taken from them? Would you completely relieve them from the Canadian tax and let them pay on the other side?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would be liable under this measure. Let us assume that a transportation company, such as my hon. 'friend has in mind, were liable here for say $500,000 or $1,000,000; let us assume that they were taxed under the Act that is referred to here for purely war purposes in Great Britain, or in France, to an amount aggregating $250,000, we should deduct $250,000 which they are obliged to pay abroad from the total amount called for by this measure, and they would pay us the balance.

Perhaps I am wrong in my statement of the case, but I have seen in one of the Western papers the statement that the Canadian Pacific would escape the taxation on account of a certain clause in their contract with the Canadian Government exempting them from taxation. Has my hon. friend read that' clause and is the Canadian Pacific exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In my view the Canadian Pacific is not exempt. There is nothing in this measure that is, in my judgment, inconsistent with, or in violation of, the legislation to vdrich my hon. friend refers, and which is contained in the statutes of the year 1881.
What is the exact bearing of that exemption of 1881?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The section to which my hon. friend refers is section 16 of the Act respecting the Canadian Pacific railway, assented to on February 15, 1881, and it is as follows:
The Canadian Pacific railway, and all stations and station grounds, workshops, buildings, yards and other property, rolling stock and appurtenances required and used for the construction and working thereof, and the capital stock of the company shall be for ever free from taxation by the Dominion, or by any province hereafter to be established, or by any municipal corporation therein, and the lands of the company in the Northwest Territories, until they are either sold or occupied, shall also be free from such taxation for 2d years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
My view >
ie that this legislation is not inconsistent with or in violation of the section which I have read. I think it is only fair to say that in so far as I am aware the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is not desirous of escaping the obligation of paying this war taxation. Would the committee oblige me by reconsidering section 2? In the second to the last line of subsection "e" of section 2 I desire to ask the committee to strike out three words, "the profits of." We are exempting the parties liable to taxation to the amount of any tax paid under any legislation for raising revenue for the present war, in force in France, Russia, Italy, Belgium, Servia, Montenegro, Japan, or the colonies or dependencies of any of these countries, in respect of the profits of any business. It was pointed out to me that in France, Belgium and England the war tax is not necessarily in respect of profits as this Bill is. If we strike out the three words the section will read,

"in respect of any business liable to taxation."
Subsection "b" of section 2 is for holding companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And subsection "a" is to provide that the amount paid under the Special War Revenue Act of 1915 shall be deducted if the banks pay more under this legislation. If they pay less, which Act applies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The existing legislation still continues to apply.
Paragraph 2, as amended, agreed to.
On paragraph 4:
That the business to which the tax shall apply are all trades and businesses (including the business of transportation), of any description carried on, or partly carried on, in Canada whether continuously or not except :
(a)	the business of any person the capital employed in which is less than fifty thousand dollars, other than a business which, or twenty per centum or more of which, is or has been the manufacturing or dealing in munitions of war or in materials or supplies of any kind for war purposes;
(b)	the business of life insurance;
(c)	the business of farming and live stock raising; and
(d)	the business of any company, commission or association not less than ninety per cent of the stock of which is owned by a province or a municipality.

In my opinion this will be the most difficult clause of all to enforce. If I understand the minister correctly, his object is to compel firms that are exclusively engaged in supplying war materials to pay a portion of their profits to the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to the difficulties he is going to encounter when he attempts to enforce this clause. For example, in the Auditor General's Report he will find certain war expenditures. I told ith-e House the other day that the patronage committees gave the names of those from whom prices . were to be asked for war supplies and these committees practically decided who should furnish them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely not.

Surely. I think I shall be able to prove to the minister that certain firms have been paid for supplying war materials, which, outside of that particular business, have no existence as firms. The individuals composing the firm may exist.
I hesitate a little about reading names, but I would draw the minister's attention to page 68 of part ZZ, Auditor General's report which shows that $3,935.67 was paid for supplies for army purposes. One of the items of that amount was 10,046 pounds of potatoes, at 44 cents a pound, which is about $7 a barrel. I do not believe that this firm exists outside of this particular transaction.
What is its name?
Armstrong & Ferguson, of Newcastle. There is now, no such firm in Newcastle.
My object in asking was that a mistake might have been made; these might have been evaporated potatoes. The price is ridiculous for ordinary potatoes.
There is no doubt about them being ordinary potatoes.

materials from its total sales? As I understand this resolution, it is to the effect that, if a firm sells in war materials, less than 20 per cent of its turnover, it does not pay anything on its sales of war materials provided it does not earn over 7 per oent profit. That is a fact according to the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

The business of any person the capital employed in which is less than $50,000-
If they sell over 20 per cent in war materials that does not apply, but if they sell less than 20 per cent, they must, to be liable for taxation, have a capital of $50,000. Is that the meaning of the subsection?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Then, a great many firms that supply war materials will not pay one cent, while small firms, such as the firm I have mentioned here, that do not do any other business than to supply war materials, must pay. A firm that supplies twenty or thirty or forty thousand dollars worth of war materials will not pay one cent if it does not have 20 per cent of its gross sales in war materials, and if its capital is under $50,000. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's statement is pretty clear. Under these resolutions, as brought down, the taxation was to apply to businesses which had a capital of at least $50,000 , and not to businesses which had a capital of less than $50,000. We made an exception, however, in the case of businesses which dealt exclusively in manufacturing war munitions or in furnishing supplies. The idea was that those businesses were making money directly out of the war, and, in many cases, the profits would be abnormal, although I do not say that that would always be the case. It was drawn to my attention that, as the resolutions were drawn, a firm which had received an -order for $500 worth of war supplies, or $26 worth in one case, but which was carrying on its business otherwise as usual, that is to say, not manufacturing for war purposes ' and not furnishing war supplies, would become liable. That, of course, seemed manifestly unfair, because the war.business was such a small proportion of the total business. It therefore seemed to us that we might fairly amend the resolution by providing that, if a company with a capital

of less than $50,000 dealt in war munitions or furnished war supplies to an amount not exceeding 20 per cent, it should be allowed to come under the provision exempting companies with a -capital of less than $50,000. As we had to fix a percentage arbitrarily, we fixed it at 20 per cent. The business of a company witn a capital of less than $50,000 is not likely to be very considerable, and 20 per cent of the gross amount did not seem to give them such a large amount of profit as should deprive them of the exemption enjoyed by other businesses.

I would like to call attention to subsection " d " of section 4, which exempts from the operations of this measure:
The business of any company, commission, or association not less than 90 per cent of the stock of which is owned by a province or a municipality.
That amendment, I think, covers a number of cases in the province of Ontario where corporations are practically owned by municipalities, and I understand the intention of the minister is that such corporations shall not be subject to the tax. I do not think that the exemption is quite broad enough in its language to include all corporations that are operated by municipalities. I have in mind at present a street railway company, an incorporated company, all the stock of which is now owned by the municipality, except a few shares to qualify a board of directors. Such a company would be included under subsection "d" because, as over 90 per cent of its stock is held by the municipality, it would not be subject to the tax; but under the Ontario Public Utilities Act there are a number of corporations created which have no capital stock. They have capital, and capital is subject to taxation under section 2, but that capital is not divided into shares. Under the Ontario Public Utilities Act, -any municipality may appoint a hydro-electric commission, a waterworks commission, or a light, heat and power commission, for the operation of the public utilities of the municipality, and that Act, declares that those commissions shall be bodies corporate. Now, I would fear that, under this section, they might be subject to taxation unless they were explicitly exempted. I would therefore suggest that words of this kind be added to subsection "d":
Or any municipal public utility commission authorized by any provincial statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the point raised by my hon. friend is well taken, and I am indebted to him for drawing my attention to the matter. The city of Guelph owns the capital stock of a street railway company, and it did not seem to me expedient that the tax should apply in such a case, and it also did not seem expedient to me that the tax should apply to a public utility corporation owned by a province. There are two points to which my hon. friend referred. As to the first, I have an amendment to propose which I think will meet the situation. I move:
That subsection " d " of section 4 be amended by adding, after the work " stock,"' the words " or capital."
If that completely covers what the hon. gentleman has in view, I need not deal with any other point. Did I understand him to say that the expression " company, commission, or association," is not wide enough? I think it is wide enough.

I think the amendment suggested by the minister will cover the case. This applies not only with regard to the city of Guelph, but to all places in which the Hydro-Electric is in operation. These commissioners, under the Public Utilities Act become corporations. They have no stock but they have capital. I think the change will cover it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I do not want to oppose the proposition, but I am surprised to hear that under the Hydro-Electric they make profits of seven per cent. I understood that in Ontario they were getting power at cost. Of course, I have always said, that I know places where private corporations sell electric energy at cheaper rates than it is sold for in Ontario. However, that is their affair.
1 wish to mention a point which has been called to my attention in three different cases, and I am sure it will be of direct interest to many throughout Canada. Subsection " a " of section 4 refers to:
The business of any person the capital employed in which is less than fifty thousand dollars.
The question I have to ask would not affect a corporation, and possibly it would not affect a partnership, as it would be assumed that all the property that the partnership hold would be employed in the conduct of the business. But take the case of a private individual who runs a business
in which he has not $50,000 invested, and who has also property in other forms-other investments. Would the term " business " in that case cover only the business that the men ordinarily carries on, or would it cover his private property as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would call the attention of my hon. friend to section 10:
The capital employed in the business of any person other than an incorporated company, shall be taken to be the fair value of all assets real and peisonal, movable and immovable.
I think that presents no difficulty. If a man had $50,000 invested in, let us say, a dry-goods business, that amount could he easily ascertained. But if he had property outside of his business, that would not be " capital " for the purposes of the Act.

I wanted the minister's opinion because, as I have said, this matter has been brought to my attention on several occasions. I agree with the minister;
I think he has given a proper definition.

Why should not the rule apply to an individual as well as to a company? If the company were running a business and had a house in the town rented, that would not be counted the same as in the case of similar property owned by a private individual. Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A company is incorporated for the purpose of carrying on a business. What business it can carry on will depend upon its corporate powers. What it would he liable on would be the net profits made in carrying on its business.

I do not think it is a very important point, but I cannot see why a corporation should have more power tljan a person. A person can carry on a grocery and have a house in the town rented, and the house is not counted part of his capital. But the minister says that if an incorporated company has a house that is part of its capital.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Why should an
incorporated company have a house? If part of its business is the holding of real estate for profit, the house would be a part of its corporate enterprise, part of its business. On the other hand, my hon. friend might own real estate in Manitoba, and he might have a business in the East-and I am told he has a very fine business in the East-but the taxation measure would apply only to the amount of capital he has in the business and not to his property holdings

in Manitoba. But if he were to incorporate a company with power to hold, deal in and speculate in real estate, to carry on a hardware business and run electric tram cars- one of these companies whose charters go through here in a few minutes on Friday nights-^we would have to deal with that on its merits and count all its operations as . part of its business.

The minister deals with
a supposed company, but I want him to come down to facts. Not only might a company have a house rented outside of its regular business, but it is a common practice. There are two companies in my own town that have several houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Part of their
business.

I do not see why the minister cannot be consistent. Why apply one principle to a person and another to an incorporated company? I do not think the point is a very material one, but I would like to see the minister consistent.

In the case of an incorporated company, whose sole business is holding real estate, and having capital of $50,000, there would be no question as to *its liability. But take the case of an individual, who owns, say, $100,000 of real estate in the form of buildings. He has no other occupation than the collection of rents. Would he say that that person was conducting a business which, under the resolution, would make him liable to taxation?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has asked a question about a matter that is within the penumbral region sf light and shade, on the one side business and on the other non-business. I should think it would be a question of fact. I do not think any practical difficulty is likely to arise. If an individual were engaged in the real estate business or in buying and selling and renting property-
Supposing he was an aged man of 99 years and could not conduct the business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If he wae an aged man of 99 years, I would be disposed to let him off altogether. I think if it were his business he would be liable to act, but in the case of a private individual holding some real estate here and there 
throughout the country and deriving some revenue from it, it would haidly be described as business.
If incorporated it would.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point is that when a company is incorporated it is incorporated to do business. Every company is carrying on some sort of business in the exercise of its corporate powers.
It might be incorporated merely to hold real estate and not to deal in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then I suppose the Act might not apply because it would not earn the necessary amount. But if the property appreciated to such an extent that its earnings were sufficient to bring it within the provisions of the Act, then probably the Act might apply.
Carried.

I do not want that clause to carry; that is an awful clause. I think the minister ought not to press clause 4, subsection "a", to-night. The minister has not touched on the suggestion I mad,e to him-and I am making this suggestion merely on the strength of what he has told the committee the object of this legislation is-namely, that those who have made large profits from war supplies should pay a portion of the tax. What I urge is that a very, very large portion of the war supplies, in small amounts, will not pay any tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In small amounts.
A very large amount in the aggregate will not pay. I see one firm here in Fredericton who have supplied $4,951.59. If their sales are not 20 per cent of the business they do not pay a cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not a very large amount.
I know it is not, but in the aggregate it will be a very large amount.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me why he should pay?
If the minister will accept a suggestion of mine he will pay.
I want to know why he should pay.
The minister said he should pay.
I want to know why.

One of the objects of the legislation was to get at those who supplied material for the war on which they made a good profit. Why would the minister not consider taxing the sales, ' 10 p.m. say, a quarter of one per cent, or one-half of one per cent, or one per cent?-tax the war supplies according to the amount sold. He has records of all these sales, and then he could deduct the amount of the tax so collected from the tax collected under this resolution in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is very solicitous for the minister. He stated a while ago that I should be surrounded with difficulties. I desire to tell him that that is the normal position of my official life, and therefore he must not be unduly anxious about it. I did consider the proposal put forward by my hon. friend, which only goes to show that intellects sometimes think alike. It would lead to manifest hardship. In some cases, to my knowledge firms supplied goods at cost; and since the War Commission has been established, from inquiry I have made I am quite sure that the profits have been certainly not abnormal; the profits have been normal, reasonable, and in many instances low. The attempt to tax all parties who have been engaged in manufacturing munitions and supplying goods, on a percentage basis, would lead in some cases to actual loss to those supplying the goods. I did give the matter consideration as I said, and for the reason I have now given I came to the conclusion that it would be unfair and unjust to adopt a percentage basis. Therefore, at the risk of some trouble-because we are born and live to meet and overcome trouble-I thought it proper that the section should remain as drafted, rather than that <a percentage basis should be established.
I am going to suggest, as this is Friday night and some members are leaving town, that if the committee feel disposed to pass section 4 with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), and concurred in by the committee, we should adjourn and take up the matter again on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall this clause
carry?
No, not carried.
I thought that the motion of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition relating to shells was to come up on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that there has been any arrangement to that effect. If that has been arranged by the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition, of course the arrangement will be carried out; but I am desirous of getting these resolutions put through, and I would say that it is the intention to go on with them on Tuesday.

I have no objection; I
was only pointing out that when the House adjourned on Tuesday last that was the understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there was an understanding between the Government and the Opposition with regard to going on with the resolution relating to the Shell Committee on Tuesday, of course we shall go on; but if that is not the case, the Government desire to go on with the consideration of these resolutions. It is over a month since the Budget was brought down, and the Government can hardly be considered to have acted unreasonably with regard to the resolutions before the House.

I would like to ask the
minister if he would not allow that clause to remain over until Monday, and think the matter over? I was very much interested in the minister's explanation that war supplies had been given at cost price. That, of course, I did not anticipate; it puzzled me in a way. After all, and over and above it all, I am persuaded that the suggestion I have offered to the minister is the easiest one to meet, and provides the more equitable way of the two in the interest of all concerned. He would get a considerable revenue from it, and I certainly think it is worth considering.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would prefer,
if the House concurs in the view, that section 4 be passed, and if, on thinking it over on Tuesday, or when the House resumes consideration of the resolutions, I feel myself persuaded by the arguments of my hon. friend, I will ask the House to re-open the matter.

If a contract for war
supplies is given to a Canadian, and is carried out by an American firm, would that American firm be liable to taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the contract was carried out in the United, States by a United States company it is evident that we would have no jurisdiction to reach that company.
Could the Government not keep from the amount to be paid to the American firm a share of the profits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is no doubt aware that we have not paid American firms anything. Everything that has been paid, or will be paid, for contracts placed by the Shell Committee, or by the Munitions Board, is, or will be, paid by the Imperial Government.

I know that the Canadian Government has no jurisdiction over American companies, but in the case of a contract which is given to a person in Canada for war supplies, and which is handed over to an American concern, whether it be to Schwab or to any other concern, the payment is made by Canad,a. Would the .Canadian Government not be justified, when making payment under the contract, in retaining a certain amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is a lawyer of renown, and is acquainted with the principles of international law. He would have to consider the locus of the contract. I do not admit that the Canadian Government have made such a contract, but assume that the Canadian Government did make a contract with an American firm, in the state of New York, or anywhere else in the United States-a contract for the delivery of fuses or of munitions of any kind-upon payment under the terms of an express contract would the Government of Canada be authorized to ,say: We shall not pay that amount; we are going to deduct a certain amount because we need to raise revenue in the Dominion. My hon. friend will see that international questions would at once arise.

I do not suppose that the minister would object to those members who have views in regard to this section bringing them forward, on Tuesday, even if we consider the section to be passed?
Sir THOMAS. WHITE: I have so much regard for this committee that any reasonable request will be met readily and with pleasure.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
Progress reported.
